items.title: Sahasrara
level: The top level is in charge of the link to a bigger plan: why any of this, and what stays behind afterwards. While it keeps quiet a person lives perfectly well, but every so often runs into the question “and what then” — and no pay rise ever answers it.

A strong Sahasrara gives the calm of someone who knows their place in something larger: they do not shrink into squabbles and tell the important from the merely urgent. An empty one pulls either into cynicism (“there is nothing”) or into somebody else’s teaching, where ready-made meaning is handed out at the door.
items.personal_intro: Values and meaning: your actions, inner motivation and feelings about the path you choose.

columns.title: Physics
columns.text: In matter this is about the end result: which of a person’s deeds outlive them — what they wrote, what they built, the people they taught. The same column shows whether they manage to do anything not only for themselves.

columns.title: Energy
columns.text: Gives a reserve of meaning that strength is drawn from in the hard years. With that reserve a person comes through losses without falling apart; with none, they break on the first serious injustice.

columns.title: Emotions
columns.text: Felt as quiet gratitude and a sense that life is not an accident. Out of balance it turns into either exaltation and an endless search for a teacher, or a cold emptiness in which everything looks pointless.

article.title: Sahasrara in the destiny matrix: the seventh chakra you share with everyone born on your birthday
article.short: Sahasrara is the seventh chakra, the one at the very top. In our table it ends the climb from footing to meaning. Its theme is meaning and direction: what you spend your strength on, what you lean on when you choose a path, and how it feels to walk it. Its row holds three arcana: physics is the arcanum of your birth day, energy is the number of your birth month, emotions is their sum. It is the only chakra whose calculation leaves the year out. You can work it out in ten seconds straight from the date on a birthday cake, and it is exactly the same for everyone born on your day. Below: the calculation, the meaning of all 22 arcana in each column, worked examples of real triples, and what the full chakra reading says about yours.

sections.h2: How to work out your Sahasrara in ten seconds

ol: **Physics — the day’s arcanum.** If you were born between the 1st and the 22nd, take the number as it is. From the 23rd on, add the digits: 23 → 5, 24 → 6, 25 → 7, 26 → 8, 27 → 9, 28 → 10, 29 → 11, 30 → 3, 31 → 4.
**Energy — the month.** Its number from 1 to 12, with no conversion at all.
**Emotions — the sum.** Add the first two numbers. If the result is over 22, add its digits: 15 + 12 = 27 → 9.

paragraphs: You can read energy straight off your birth month:

ul: **31 March:** 31 → 4 (The Emperor), March is 3 (The Empress), 4 + 3 = 7 (The Chariot). The Sahasrara is **4 / 3 / 7** — exactly the same as for anyone born on 4 March.
**15 July:** 15 (The Devil), 7 (The Chariot), 15 + 7 = 22 (The Fool) — **15 / 7 / 22**.
**29 November:** 29 → 11 (Strength), November is 11 (Strength), 11 + 11 = 22 (The Fool) — **11 / 11 / 22**, the same as for those born on 11 November.
**22 December:** 22 (The Fool), 12 (The Hanged Man), 22 + 12 = 34 → 7 (The Chariot) — **22 / 12 / 7**.

paragraphs: Your triple matches, number for number, the triple of everyone born on the same day and month — in 1950, 1990 or 2010. The other six rows take the birth year into account as well, and most of them first need the centre of the chart and its inner points. So the day and month alone do not settle the whole matrix. Why it works this way, and what follows from it, is below. The order of writing never changes: “physics / energy / emotions”.

sections.h2: What Sahasrara is: from the thousand-petalled lotus to the question “what for?”
paragraphs: The name is Sanskrit: sahasrāra means “thousand-petalled”. It is the lotus at the crown of the head — the highest of the centres described in Indian tantric texts. The best known of these in the West is Purnananda’s treatise Shat-chakra-nirupana of 1577, that is, “Description of the Six Chakras”. Europe came to know it through the English translation by John Woodroffe, published under the pen name Arthur Avalon in The Serpent Power (1919).

Look closely at that title: the treatise counts six chakras, from Muladhara to Ajna. Sahasrara stands “above all these”. It is a lotus of a thousand petals, “lustrous and whiter than the full Moon”, with its head turned downward; its body is “luminous with the letters beginning with A”. The classical scheme does not usually put it in line with the other chakras: it is the summit the whole path leads to. The familiar row of seven, with Sahasrara in seventh place, spread around the world through Western books of the twentieth century. That is also when the chakras were painted in the colours of the rainbow and Sahasrara was given violet. The treatise itself says not a word about violet.

Benebell Wen’s Holistic Tarot (2015) includes a Seven Chakras spread. Its seventh card, the Crown, speaks of karma, unfinished business, higher consciousness and the connection with the divine. Wen adds a line that captures the spirit of the position better than anything else: “In practical application, Card 7 indicates the Seeker in his or her best possible manifestation.” In her spread the card is drawn from the deck rather than calculated from a date, so it does not carry straight over into the matrix. But the direction is the same: Sahasrara is about the highest point a person is able to reach.

In our reading, Sahasrara completes the climb through the seven chakras. Its theme is “Meaning and direction”, and its hint is “connection to a larger plan”. We read it in practical terms. Sahasrara does not measure spirituality and does not ask what you believe. It asks what makes the effort worth it for you: what a piece of work has to hold for it to feel like yours, what you lean on when you choose a direction, and what you feel along your road. The question matters just as much to a believer as to an atheist, to a monk as to an entrepreneur — they simply answer it differently.

sections.h2: Sahasrara’s three numbers: the deed, the anchor, the feeling
paragraphs: The row reads as one thought in three steps: **what I do for what matters → what leads me to it → how it feels to be on this path**.

**Physics — deeds.** This is where the arcanum of your birth day goes: the same point A that the matrix calls the calling card. In the general reading, the calling card describes the first impression a person makes. In Sahasrara the question is different: how your values look from the outside. Values show not in words but in decisions — what you spend an evening on, what you turn down, what you take on without being talked into it. The test is simple: remember what you did the last time something truly important was at stake.

**Energy — the anchor.** Here stands the month of birth — point B, which the matrix calls the spiritual task. It is the source that meaning is drawn from: a teaching, the people close to you, your own experience, order, freedom, moving towards a goal. Energy is easiest to notice when it runs short. When meaning drains away and everything is done on autopilot, what exactly has gone missing? That is usually your anchor.

**Emotions — how the path feels.** The third number is the reduced sum of the first two, and that is not a technicality. The feeling of a path arises where deeds meet the anchor: uplift, calm, excitement, anxiety, a quiet “yes”. So emotions do not grade whether your beliefs are right. They show how a life feels when you are doing what is worth the effort — and how its absence makes itself felt.
No column is the main one. Physics without energy turns into busyness, energy without physics into daydreams, and emotions without the other two into a mood with no cause.

sections.h2: Why everyone born on your day has the same Sahasrara
paragraphs: The destiny matrix has more than twenty calculated points, and all but three of them pass through the birth year: directly, through the year point, or through the centre of the chart, where the year is one of the terms. We checked this both against the formulas and by running through every date from 1940 to 2012. Only the day arcanum A, the month B and their sum F do not depend on the year — exactly the three numbers of Sahasrara. The Sahasrara row is built from the only numbers in the chart that stay the same from year to year.
A few things follow from this that are rarely written about.

ul: **You have “Sahasrara twins”.** Everyone born on 15 July gets 15 / 7 / 22, whether in 1950 or in 2010. Their other six chakras differ, and those differences are what make each chart its own.

**The top and bottom of the table mirror each other.** Sahasrara starts from the day and month — the numbers people celebrate as a birthday. The bottom chakra, Muladhara, starts from the year arcanum: its physics is shared by everyone born in the same year. Personal at the top, generational at the bottom.

**Sahasrara is the first thirty years on the age scale.** The scale goes round the octagram, ten years per point: from birth to 10 the day arcanum A leads, from 10 to 20 point F, from 20 to 30 the month B. These are the same three numbers, only in a different order: physics, emotions, energy. The match is pure arithmetic, but it fits the theme neatly: these are just the decades in which a person usually puts together a world-view. First you simply live and act, then you feel things sharply, then you choose what to lean on.

**Each Sahasrara number does another job elsewhere.** On the diagram the first two are the left and top corners of the personal square, and the third sits between them, in a corner of the family square. Physics is the calling card, energy is the spiritual task, and the section on the family line reads the sum as the spiritual male family line. These are different questions put to the same number, and what the number means in Sahasrara does not carry over to them.

sections.h2: Which triples are common and which almost never happen
paragraphs: All the figures below come from running through 26,664 birth dates from 1940 to 2012. Since the year does not enter Sahasrara, the picture is practically the same for any other period.

ul: **There are 264 triples in all, and every one of them occurs**: 22 options for physics times 12 months. Each day of the calendar has exactly one triple.

**Physics from 3 to 11 turns up almost twice as often as the rest.** These arcana get two days a month: the 5th and the 23rd give the same number, and so do the 7th and the 25th. That is why 4 / 3 / 7 belongs to people born on both 4 and 31 March, while 22 / 12 / 7 belongs only to those born on 22 December.

**Arcana 13 to 22 never stand in energy**: there are only twelve months. Death, The Star, The Sun or The World reach Sahasrara only through deeds or feelings. The anchor of meaning here always comes from the first twelve arcana — from The Magician to The Hanged Man.

**The Magician never appears in emotions, and The High Priestess almost never.** A sum of two numbers never reduces to 1, and 2 can only come from 1 + 1. The High Priestess stands in Sahasrara’s emotions for people born on 1 January — and for no one else.
**Strength is the most frequent arcanum in emotions** — 6.6% of dates. After The High Priestess, the rarest are The Empress (1.9%) and The Emperor (2.2%).

**The Fool appears in emotions only when the sum is exactly 22.** That means 21 January, 20 February, 19 March, 18 April, 17 May, 16 June, 15 July, 14 August, 13 September, 12 October, 11 and 29 November, 10 and 28 December. The later the month, the earlier the day — like a countdown.

**The Moon as a mirror.** For people born on the 18th from May to November, emotions repeat energy: 18 / 5 / 5, 18 / 6 / 6 and so on up to 18 / 11 / 11. That is how reduction works: 18 + 9 = 27, and 2 + 7 gives 9 again. There is no other way to get a copy of one of the columns in emotions. A coincidence that is hard to miss: for Waite, The Moon is the card of reflected light.

**Repeats are rare.** Physics equals energy on the twelve “mirror” dates, from 01/01 to 12/12, and also for those born on 30 March, 23 May, 24 June, 25 July, 26 August, 27 September, 28 October and 29 November. Together with the Moon mirror, that makes 19 triples out of 264, or 7.4% of dates. A repeat does not mean doubling: one number simply answers two different questions.
**The Chariot turns up in one calculated Sahasrara in five** — 20% of dates. Any arcanum from 5 to 11 scores about the same. Arcana 13 to 22 appear here 2–3 times less often: on 7 to 9% of dates.

sections.h2: The 22 arcana in Sahasrara, column by column
paragraphs: Find your three numbers and read the columns you need. Under each arcanum’s name it says who has it in physics and who has it in energy. The descriptions are symbolic themes for Sahasrara, not ready-made verdicts on character. A whole picture only comes from all three numbers together; how to put them together is in the next section.
Physics — for those born on the 1st, energy — January. Never appears in emotions.

ul: **Physics:** meaning is tested by doing. You take whatever is at hand and begin, without waiting for ideal conditions or anyone’s permission. Taken too far: believing that will decides everything and any plan comes true if you try hard enough.
**Energy:** the anchor is your own decision and the feeling of “I can”. Meaning appears where you set something going yourself, and fades when you are cast as the executor of someone else’s plan.

paragraphs: Physics — the 2nd, energy — February, emotions — only for those born on 1 January.

ul: **Physics:** you rarely announce your values, but they show in your choices — above all in what you quietly do not do. Understand first, act second. Taken too far: waiting for full clarity when it is already time to decide.
**Energy:** the answer to “what for?” comes in silence, not in argument. The anchor is inner knowing; it is worth telling it apart from an anxious hunch and checking it against the facts.
**Emotions:** the path feels like a quiet inner “yes” that is hard to put into words.

paragraphs: Physics — the 3rd and the 30th, energy — March.

ul: **Physics:** your values take shape in things that grow: a home, a project, a garden, the people around you. You create conditions in which living things get stronger. Taken too far: growing everything at once and running out of breath from your own generosity.
**Energy:** the anchor is fruitfulness. There is meaning when your efforts make something appear and develop; without visible shoots it fades fast.
**Emotions:** fullness when work bears fruit, and emptiness when the fruit is long in coming. In Sahasrara’s emotions The Empress is a rarity, under 2% of dates.

paragraphs: Physics — the 4th and the 31st, energy — April.

ul: **Physics:** you give your values a form: rules, routine, commitments that get kept. A principle, for you, is something that works every day, not only in conversation. Taken too far: the rule outlives its point and is kept out of habit.
**Energy:** the anchor is independence and responsibility. Meaning lies where you are the author of the decision and answer for the result.
**Emotions:** calm confidence when everything is set up as it should be; irritation when others live by different rules.

paragraphs: Physics — the 5th and the 23rd, energy — May.

ul: **Physics:** you pass on what matters: you teach, explain, keep a tradition — of a family, a profession or a faith. Waite named the main trap of this card: the bearer of a teaching may forget “the significance of this his symbolic state” and act “as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies”.

**Energy:** the anchor is a tested system of values, a mentor, your own circle. Meaning is sturdier when it is shared with people who think alike. Now and then it is worth asking yourself why this principle matters to you personally.
**Emotions:** a sense of belonging and of being in the right; tension when the people close to you see things differently.

paragraphs: Physics — the 6th and the 24th, energy — June.

ul: **Physics:** values are tested by choice: who to go with, what for, what to give up. Taken too far: putting off the choice so as not to lose anyone.

**Energy:** the anchor is the people close to you and agreement on what matters most. Meaning lives in connection; it is important to tell your own conviction apart from the wish to be in step with others.
**Emotions:** joy when heart and choice say the same thing; wavering when you have to choose between two things you hold dear.

paragraphs: Physics — the 7th and the 25th, energy — July.

ul: **Physics:** meaning turns into a route: a goal, stages, obstacles overcome. Taken too far: racing ahead without asking whether it is the right way.
**Energy:** the anchor is a landmark that pulls you. Without a direction meaning fades, even when everything is fine.
**Emotions:** a lift from making progress and frustration when you have to stand still. More on the seven in a separate section below.

paragraphs: Physics — the 8th and the 26th, energy — August.

ul: **Physics:** your values show in honesty and in readiness to answer for the consequences. One measure for yourself and for others. Taken too far: turning every mistake of your own into a verdict.
**Energy:** the anchor is a clear sense of what is right. Meaning lies where things are fair; injustice knocks the ground from under you harder than failure does.
**Emotions:** inner agreement when the choice is honest; guilt or resentment when the balance is broken.

paragraphs: Physics — the 9th and the 27th, energy — September.

ul: **Physics:** you get to the heart of things on your own — and then share what you found: you teach, advise, write. Waite insisted that the Hermit is not searching but has already found: his beacon intimates that “where I am, you also may be”. Taken too far: going so deep into the search that the conclusion never reaches people.
**Energy:** the anchor is your own experience. Other people’s ready answers do not convince you until you have tested them yourself.
**Emotions:** the calm of an answer found; loneliness if the path seems clear only to you.

paragraphs: Physics — the 10th and the 28th, energy — October.

ul: **Physics:** you rebuild your plans when life takes a turn and still keep the main thing — you can tell a lasting value from the passing form of a task. Taken too far: blaming circumstances for what was your own choice.
**Energy:** the anchor is a sense of pattern. Meaning shows not at a single point but across a cycle: rise, fall, a new turn.
**Emotions:** curiosity about a new stage; bewilderment when it seems that nothing depends on you.

paragraphs: Physics — the 11th and the 29th, energy — November.

ul: **Physics:** you stand up for your principles gently and for a long time: without shouting, but without giving way on what matters most. Taken too far: putting up with things when it is time to say “no”.

**Energy:** the anchor is self-command. Meaning grows stronger when you manage to master your own fear or anger, not someone else’s resistance. In Waite the lion “is being led by a chain of flowers”: what holds it is not force but a law “taken into the heart of hearts”.

**Emotions:** dignity and inner quiet when you have stayed true to yourself; anger when someone else’s disagreement feels like a challenge. These are Sahasrara’s most frequent emotions — 6.6% of dates.

paragraphs: Physics — the 12th, energy — December.

ul: **Physics:** you can stop and look at things differently from the usual way — give up the obvious for the sake of what matters. Waite stressed that the Hanged Man’s tree is “living wood” and that “the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”: this is “life in suspension”, not martyrdom. Taken too far: getting stuck in the pause.
**Energy:** the anchor is an unfamiliar angle. Meaning comes when you stop rushing the answer.
**Emotions:** acceptance and a quiet clarity after your view has turned upside down; helplessness if the waiting drags on.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 13th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you know how to close chapters: walk away from what is exhausted, drop beliefs that are no longer yours. Taken too far: cutting before it is clear what exactly is leaving.
**Emotions:** sadness and relief at the same time. New meaning does not come at once, and that is a normal part of the transition.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 14th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** meaning lies in joining the different parts of life: work and home, faith and doubt, old experience and new. Taken too far: a compromise with none of your own choice left in it.
**Emotions:** the calm of having found your measure and pace; boredom if the measure has eaten up the excitement.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 15th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you honestly admit what you want — success, influence, money, pleasure — and put a great deal of strength into it. The card does not turn into a “talent for making money” here: its question remains a question of dependence. Which of the things you want holds you, rather than you holding it?
**Emotions:** a strong pull — towards recognition, a goal, a person. Excitement and the fear of losing live side by side; the same fire that drives you forward can become a chain.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 16th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you are ready to tear down your own picture of the world if the facts have disproved it. For Waite the Tower is above all “the rending of a House of Doctrine” — or, more precisely, of “a House of Falsehood” — and not a punishment for pride. Taken too far: smashing everything instead of what really gave way.
**Emotions:** a sharp collapse of certainty that may later turn into relief. The risk is declaring all your past experience a mistake.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 17th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you give a dream the shape of a small, generous act: you share, inspire, support those who have lost their way. Waite dismissed “hope” as “the summary of several tawdry explanations” and saw in the Star “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. Taken too far: waiting for the ideal to come true on its own.
**Emotions:** inspiration and a quiet faith in the future; disappointment when the first step is too far from the picture.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 18th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you explore what is frightening and unclear: dreams, fears, hunches, the dark corners of your own story. Waite drew a clear line: the card stands for “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”, and the Moon’s light is only reflected. Taken too far: mistaking anxiety for knowledge.
**Emotions:** a fine sensitivity to questions of meaning and an unease without a name. It helps to turn a vague anxiety into a concrete question.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 19th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** your values are out in the open: you do what matters in plain sight, generously and with pleasure, and the people around you feel brighter for it. Taken too far: resentment when your light goes unnoticed.
**Emotions:** the clear joy of taking part; hurt when your contribution is recognised less than you expected.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 20th. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you answer a call — a vocation, an important cause, your family’s story — and you know how to take stock. Waite framed the question of this card like this: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response?” Taken too far: living by someone else’s call instead of your own.
**Emotions:** a sense of “this is mine” and of responsibility to the people close to you; anxiety when the call cannot be heard.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 21st. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** you gather experience into a whole picture and see things through to the end. Taken too far: in the wide view, what is close at hand gets lost.
**Emotions:** a sense of connection with the wider world; detachment from simple things if breadth crowds out involvement.

paragraphs: Physics — for those born on the 22nd. Never appears in energy.

ul: **Physics:** meaning is found by trying. You are ready to learn anew and to start without a finished picture of the world. In Waite the Fool is “the spirit in search of experience”, not a simpleton at all. Taken too far: any constancy starts to feel like a cage.
**Emotions:** lightness and curiosity before the unknown; anxiety when you have to choose once and for all. The Fool stands here only if physics and the month add up to exactly 22.

sections.h2: How to turn three numbers into one thought
paragraphs: The reference above gives you three themes. But a person lives not three themes but one life, and interpretation begins where the numbers come together in a single sentence.

ol: **Name each arcanum’s contribution to the theme of meaning.** Not all its meanings at once, but one — the one that answers the column’s question.
**Find the link.** The anchor may feed the deeds, or it may argue with them; emotions show how that meeting resonates. A link is support, tension or a sequence, not the sum of three character traits.
**Write one sentence: “What matters to me is…”** If it would fit anyone at all, you have not yet taken one of the numbers into account.
**Look for the difficulty in the same logic.** It grows out of a strength that has gone too far, not out of a “bad card”.

paragraphs: Below are three examples. The first is an excerpt from our full chakra reading: this is how the section looks to a person with this triple. The other two we have worked through briefly, to show the line of thought itself.

paragraphs.h3: 4 / 3 / 7 — 4 and 31 March: how the section looks in the full reading

paragraphs: **Making something you recognise yourself in**

In Sahasrara, independence meets meaning: you need to know what you are giving your strength for. The Emperor sets up the wish to shape your own life — to choose what you answer for, which rules you accept and what counts as a result. The Empress fills this with substance: you want to create, to develop, to make things better. The Chariot adds a sense of your own direction — the satisfaction of moving where you yourself decided to go.

**You need to be the author of what you put yourself into.** A piece of work comes alive when it carries your own idea and a chance to influence the result. It might be a project of your own, work within a team or making a home — the scale is secondary. What matters is the recognition itself: “This is what I wanted to make. Now it exists, and I care how it turned out.” The fruits of your labour become part of your life, and you feel the effort was not wasted.

Meaning starts to slip away when the next goal turns up before you have had time to enjoy what you achieved. Bigger, faster, harder — and soon it is difficult to remember what it was all for. Even a good result instantly becomes a step towards the next one. You keep moving, but the feeling of fullness keeps getting postponed. That is when it shows most clearly how much you need to see the tangible good of what you have done: what has come into being, who is better off, what can now be used and treasured.

The Chariot stands here twice, and Temperance sets the feelings. The anchor is a landmark that pulls you: without a goal that matters, your strength drains away into the sand. Deeds turn that landmark into a route — stages, decisions, obstacles taken one after another. Temperance governs when the road starts to feel good: when drive joins with measure, and the big goal does not burn out the rest of your life.

**The thought that comes out of it: you take on big things not in a rush but as a road that lasts for years.** A new profession, a business of your own, a serious skill — you do not throw yourself at them so hard that you burn out in a month, and you do not put them off until better times. You find a rhythm with room for the goal, for rest and for people.

The difficulty grows out of that same measure. When the goal demands more than usual, you are tempted to make it “more realistic”: push back the deadline, scale down the ambition. Each adjustment is reasonable, but together they slowly whittle down the landmark itself, and one day it stops calling. The movement is steady, but the excitement it all began with is gone.

The Tower in deeds frightens many people, but in this triple it means something else. The anchor here is The Hermit: you trust what you have understood yourself, through your own experience. So what you are ready to take apart is not just anything, but exactly what experience has disproved. In this pairing the Tower is the ability to tear down your own picture of the world when the facts are against it, without clinging to the years you have invested. The Chariot in feelings gives the sense that after the collapse the road goes on rather than rolling back.

**The thought: your meaning grows stronger through honest revisions.** An approach to your work that you built up over years one day fails to survive contact with reality. You go away to think, find where the mistake was, and come back with a more precise understanding — and with experience worth sharing.

The difficulty is that the revision is lived through alone, while The Chariot immediately calls you forward. Going back and saying out loud “I was wrong back then” feels like stopping. People who were following your earlier conclusions are the last to learn they no longer stand. And trust is lost then not because of the mistake but because it was kept quiet.

sections.h2: 7 in Sahasrara: the seventh chakra and The Chariot
paragraphs: A search like “Sahasrara 7” can mean two things, and both readings are right.

**Sahasrara is the seventh chakra.** Counting from the bottom, it closes the row: Muladhara, Svadhisthana, Manipura, Anahata, Vishuddha, Ajna, Sahasrara. In our table and in the full reading it comes last: the reading climbs from Muladhara to Sahasrara, from footing to meaning. In the sixteenth-century treatise, as we saw, there are six chakras, with Sahasrara above them; it was the Western tradition that made it the seventh.

**Seven as a number in the row is The Chariot.** It can stand in any column: in physics for those born on the 7th and the 25th, in energy for those born in July, in emotions when physics and the month add up to 7, 25 or 34 — for example on 4 March, 16 September or 22 December. Together that is one birth date in five.

The Chariot in Sahasrara is meaning through movement. Waite describes the charioteer as a victor: “He has led captivity captive; he is conquest on all planes—in the mind, in science, in progress.” And at once he sets a limit: the planes of his conquest are “manifest or external and not within himself”, and the liberation he brings to others may leave him “in the bondage of the logical understanding”. For the chakra of meaning this is a very precise question. The Chariot gives direction, will and speed, but does not itself answer what the journey is for. When there is an answer, the seven drives confidently and far. When there is none, movement becomes an end in itself: the next goal turns up before the last one has brought any joy.

Wen makes an observation that sounds almost symbolic for the top chakra. The eight-pointed star on the charioteer’s crown, she writes, recurs “in full bloom” in the 17th arcanum, The Star. The Chariot is about action and control; The Star is about the hope that such action will lead to success. In English, Sahasrara is called the Crown chakra — and on the charioteer’s crown there shines a star.

sections.h2: What Sahasrara does not tell you: five misreadings

ol: **“My Sahasrara is closed.”** The numbers in the table are arcanum numbers, not fill levels. All seven rows are filled for every person, and no single number lets you declare a chakra closed, empty or blocked.

**“The higher the number, the higher the spirituality.”** The Fool (22) is no more spiritual than The Magician (1), and The World (21) is no better than The Empress (3). The number is the name of a symbol, not a score.

**“Sahasrara is about religion and superpowers.”** Its question is what you live and act for. The answer may be faith, or it may be work, family, knowledge, freedom. The matrix does not check what you believe and does not measure abilities.

**“The Devil, The Tower or Death in Sahasrara is a bad sign.”** Death here is the ability to close what is exhausted, The Tower is a readiness to revise a false picture of the world. The Devil keeps its hard question about dependence, but a question is not a verdict: seeing honestly what holds you is exactly this card’s work.

**“Two identical numbers mean the quality is doubled.”** A repeat shows that one symbol answers two different questions. In 11 / 11 / 22, Strength stands both in deeds and in the anchor, but this is not “double strength”. In deeds it shows as firmness without pressure, and in the anchor as trust in yourself: fear, if it comes, can be tamed without a fight.

sections.h2: Sahasrara is the summit, not the whole chart
paragraphs: Sahasrara is three numbers out of the twenty-one in the chakra table, and the only ones that do not depend on the year. The other six rows take the birth year into account as well, so a familiar day and month do not promise a familiar matrix. Meaning does not live on its own: next to it stand footing in everyday life (Muladhara), desire (Svadhisthana), will (Manipura), closeness (Anahata), speech (Vishuddha) and understanding (Ajna).
After the calculation, the “Chakras and your arcana” table shows all 21 arcana of your matrix — free and with no sign-up. The interpretations open in the full reading. Here is what it contains:

ul: **Each of the seven chakras has its own section**: a heading, three cards with short captions and three paragraphs. The first introduces the chakra’s theme and shows what each arcanum contributes, the second brings them together into a whole picture, and the third says honestly where the same strength can start to get in the way.

**The texts are written for each triple as a whole**, not pieced together from dictionary snippets. For Sahasrara alone there are 264 of them — one for every possible combination, some 68,000 words. For all seven chakras there are 1,908 different texts: every triple that occurs among birth dates since 1900 has its own.

**The sections run from the bottom up**: from what gives you a sense of home, through desire, action, relationships, words and understanding — to the meaning that makes you want to keep going. Sahasrara completes the portrait.

sections.h2: What this guide is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme (Natalia Ladini’s method): Sahasrara is the day arcanum A, the month B and their reduced sum F; numbers over 22 are reduced by adding their digits. The statistics — frequencies, rare triples, independence from the year — come from running every date from 1940 to 2012 through the site’s formulas.
**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, revised edition 1922), and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the authors’ original English.
**Tradition** — Purnananda’s Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577) in John Woodroffe’s translation, The Serpent Power (1919).

**Linking the cards to Sahasrara’s columns** is the site’s own interpretation. Neither Waite, nor Wen, nor the Indian texts wrote about the destiny matrix or about “physics / energy / emotions” triples.
This is a symbolic model for self-reflection, not a forecast and not advice about money, relationships or well-being.

faq.q: How do you calculate Sahasrara in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Physics is the arcanum of your birth day: a number up to 22 is taken as it is; from the 23rd on, add the digits (25 → 7, 31 → 4). Energy is the number of the month. Emotions is the sum of the two; if it is over 22, add its digits. Example: 15 July gives 15 / 7 / 22. The order is always “physics / energy / emotions”.

faq.q: What does 7 mean in Sahasrara?
faq.a: Seven is The Chariot: meaning through movement and a goal that matters. In physics it belongs to those born on the 7th and the 25th, in energy to those born in July, and in emotions it appears when physics and the month add up to 7, 25 or 34. Its strength is turning meaning into a route; its difficulty is speed standing in for direction. If by “7” you mean the chakra’s number, Sahasrara is the seventh, the top one.

faq.q: Why is my Sahasrara the same as that of a friend with the same birthday?
faq.a: Because the year does not enter its calculation: Sahasrara is made up of the day arcanum, the month and their sum. This row is bound to match; the others are not, since they also depend on the year. But different years can produce an identical matrix too. For example, 4 March 1984 and 4 March 1993 share all seven rows.

faq.q: Can Sahasrara be closed or weak?
faq.a: Not in this calculation. Arcanum numbers do not measure strength or openness: everyone has three arcana in the row. It is more useful to look at how your combination shows itself: where it helps you choose a path and where it gets in the way.

faq.q: Why are there no numbers above 12 in Sahasrara’s energy?
faq.a: Energy is the number of the month, and there are twelve months. So the arcana from Death (13) to The Fool (22) reach Sahasrara only through physics or emotions. And emotions never hold The Magician: a sum of two numbers never reduces to 1.

faq.q: Why are my numbers different from another calculator’s?
faq.a: Check three things: the order of the columns, the reduction rule and the numbering. Here numbers over 22 are reduced by adding their digits (23 → 5), not by subtracting 22 (23 → 1). The Fool in this system is 22, not 0. If the method differs, the numbers differ too; the date has nothing to do with it.

faq.q: Is Sahasrara different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in any calculation of the matrix, and the reading of Sahasrara does not depend on it.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice and 11 Strength here?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering: the eighth card is Justice, the eleventh is Strength. Arthur Waite swapped them in the deck that Pamela Colman Smith drew for him and explained it in a single phrase: “for reasons which satisfy myself”. Many tarot books have followed him since. The meaning rests on the card’s name, so check interpretations from other systems by the arcanum’s name, not its number.

items.title: Ajna
level: Ajna is about seeing. Not eyesight, but the knack of working out in advance where a venture will end up, and of catching the main thing in a conversation. A strong level is recognised by what people around say: “how did you know”.

When this level is skewed, a person either distrusts their own guesses and regrets it every time afterwards, or believes any thought that arrives at night. The fix is plain and dull: check hunches against facts and keep score — after a year it is clear where the instinct is and where the worry is.

article.title: The Ajna chakra in the destiny matrix: how clarity comes to you
article.short: Ajna is the sixth chakra, the “third eye”. In the destiny matrix its theme is perception and understanding: how you make sense of what puzzles you, what makes you want to dig in, and what you feel at the edge of the known. In our table Ajna is the sixth row, between Vishuddha and Sahasrara. Physics is point O on the left ray of the matrix, between the birth day A and point J. Energy is point P on the top ray, between the month B and point K. Emotions are the sum of physics and energy. Any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Ajna has three properties that hardly anyone writes about. Its physics and energy are sums of its neighbours, Sahasrara and Vishuddha. Its energy is the same number that stands in the middle of the talent line. And The High Priestess, the great “intuitive” card of the tarot, never appears in anyone’s Ajna.

intro: You will see the three arcana of your Ajna straight after the calculation by date of birth, free and with no sign-up. The other six chakras will be right beside them.

sections.h2: Where Ajna sits in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The destiny matrix is an eight-pointed star made of two squares. Point A (the day of birth) is on the left, B (the month) at the top, C (the year) on the right and D (the sum of the first three) at the bottom. In the middle is the centre, E. A ray runs from each outer point to the centre, and the inner points lie along it. Ajna takes the second point from the edge on the left ray and on the top ray.

So the question “where is Ajna in the destiny matrix” has two answers. On the diagram, it is in the upper-left sector: point O on the day ray and point P on the month ray. In our table, it is the sixth row, just before Sahasrara.

The chakra table is a ladder laid across the points of the diagram. It starts at the outer points on the left and at the top (Sahasrara), converges on the centre (Manipura) and fans back out to the outer points on the right and at the bottom (Muladhara).

The table shows that the three upper chakras sit on two rays. The physics of each lies on the day ray, the energy on the month ray. Sahasrara stands at the very edge, Vishuddha next to the centre, and Ajna halfway between. This in-between position is more than geometry: as you will see, Ajna’s numbers are literally added up from its neighbours.

paragraphs.h3: How to work out Ajna by hand

paragraphs: There is only one rule: any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits until it is 22 or less. Take 31 March 1993 as an example.

ol: **A**, the day arcanum: 31 → 3 + 1 = 4.
**B**, the month: 3.
**C**, the year arcanum: 1 + 9 + 9 + 3 = 22.
**Physics** O = A + J = 4 + 8 = 12.

paragraphs: The Ajna row is **12 / 10 / 22**: The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune, The Fool. Gender plays no part in the calculation.

The formulas lead to a curious result. The birth year reaches Ajna only through the centre: physics depends on the day and the centre, energy on the month and the centre. So Ajna has almost no generational pattern. Between dates from the 1940s and the 1990s, the share of each arcanum in physics and energy shifts by no more than 0.3 percentage points. Compare Svadhisthana, where the shares of some cards differ between those decades by almost 10 points.

If another calculator gave you different numbers, check three things. Are the columns in the same order: physics, energy, emotions? Is the year reduced by adding its digits (1993 → 22) rather than by taking a remainder? And does the site use the same diagram? Here the calculation follows Natalia Ladini’s classic matrix with points A–T, while some sites use other formulas for the chakras.

sections.h2: What Ajna is and what it governs
paragraphs: In Sanskrit, ajna means “command” or “order”. The verb it comes from means “to notice, to understand”, and its root is the same one that gives English the word “know”. Two meanings meet in one name: to understand and to receive an instruction.

A detailed description of the chakra appears in the Shat-chakra-nirupana, a sixteenth-century treatise. In 1919 Arthur Avalon translated it into English in his book The Serpent Power. There Ajna is the lotus between the eyebrows, “like the moon, (beautifully white)”, with two petals bearing the letters Ha and Ksha. The next verse says: “Within this Lotus dwells the subtle mind (Manas).” And the commentary explains the name: this is where the ajna, the command of the guru, is received, the command “which is communicated from above”. The familiar blue or violet colour comes from the Western “rainbow” scheme of the chakras; in the treatise the lotus is white.

Among tarot authors, Benebell Wen uses the chakras in Holistic Tarot (2015). In her words, the sixth card of the seven chakras spread gives a sense of how a person thinks: their “clarity of thought, insights, wisdom, reason, and intuition”. Intuition is one word out of five here. That is an important correction to the popular image of Ajna as the chakra of clairvoyance.

In the readings on our site, Ajna’s theme is **perception and understanding**. It is not your level of intelligence and not a gift of foresight, but the route by which clarity reaches you: through a diagram or a trial run, through a teacher or your own experience, through an argument, a pause or a sudden image. And also what you feel while clarity has yet to come.
What Ajna in the matrix does not show: IQ, education, how accurate your hunches are, “psychic powers”, eyesight or physical wellbeing. The numbers describe a way of understanding, not how good it is.

sections.h2: Three numbers, three questions about understanding
paragraphs: **Energy (P): what switches on your interest.** Why you want to dig in at all: a clear structure, depth, novelty, mystery, an honest answer, a project moving forward. Energy decides which questions get your attention. For the rest there is never quite enough, however hard you try.

**Physics (O): how you work things out.** Your working method, what you actually do when faced with something you don’t understand. You draw a diagram, look for a textbook, try it straight away, go off to think alone, ask other people, turn the question upside down.

**Emotions (O + P): what you feel at the edge of the understood.** How you live through uncertainty, a mistake, and the moment the picture comes together: calm, excitement, anxiety, lightness, a jolt. This number is built from the first two, and that makes sense: the feeling depends both on what drew you in and on how you worked it out.
On the site the columns run in the order “physics / energy / emotions”, but they are easier to read starting from energy. First a question hooks you, then you work it out, then the feeling arrives.

**Test it on one puzzle.** Remember the last time you really got to the bottom of something: a new job, a tangled contract, the odd behaviour of someone close. What stopped you from giving up? That is energy. What did you do to work it out? That is physics. What did you feel while the picture wouldn’t come together, and at the moment it did? Those are emotions. Read against one real episode, the three arcana say far more than any reference book.
When people say “I’m slow on the uptake” or “my intuition doesn’t work”, they usually mean one of three failures. Each one falls on its own column.

ul: **“I can’t get into it.”** A failure of energy: the question doesn’t touch what really draws you. Someone with The Hierophant in energy finds it hard to learn without a system and a teacher. Someone with The Fool finds it hard to learn from a set programme where nothing can be asked afresh.

**“I keep going round in circles.”** A failure of physics: the method doesn’t suit the task, or it switches on out of habit. A diagram where a trial step is needed. Endless trials where a diagram is needed. Solitary pondering where one question to someone who knows would do.

**“I understand, but I don’t trust myself.”** A failure of emotions: not knowing feels like a threat. Then the conclusion comes too early, just to end the unpleasant wait. Or it never comes at all, because any conclusion can be challenged.

paragraphs: Your three arcana suggest what each failure looks like in your case. That is why in the full reading the difficulty of each row is drawn from its combination rather than taken from a general list.

sections.h2: Ajna sits between meaning and speech
paragraphs: The chakra table is built so that Ajna’s numbers are sums of its neighbours. This follows directly from the formulas of the method:

ul: **Ajna’s physics = Sahasrara’s physics + Vishuddha’s physics**, because O = A + J;
**Ajna’s energy = Sahasrara’s energy + Vishuddha’s energy**, because P = B + K;
**emotions** are then calculated from Ajna’s own finished numbers: O + P.

paragraphs: Here is how it looks for 31.03.1993:

From here on this is our reading, not a rule of the method. Sahasrara is about what you live for and what matters to you. Vishuddha is about how you express yourself and get your thought across to others. Ajna stands between them, and that is exactly the right place for understanding. A thought cut off from what matters to you hangs in the air. A thought that cannot be spoken stays a vague feeling. Understanding is the moment when what matters becomes clear enough to be put into words.

paragraphs.h3: Ajna’s energy is the middle of the talent line

paragraphs: The talent line in the matrix runs along the top ray: B–P–K. Look closely and you will see that it is the energy column of the three upper chakras: the month B is Sahasrara’s energy, P is Ajna’s energy, K is Vishuddha’s energy. For 31.03.1993 the talent line is 3–10–7, and its middle number, 10, is the same as Ajna’s energy.

In the talent section the middle arcanum is treated as the main one: it shows the form in which the gift unfolds. Our reading: what you are curious to understand and how your gift unfolds are described by one and the same card. That is why work that gives your curiosity nothing to catch on wears you out faster than hard work. If you have already looked at your talent line, you know your Ajna energy: it is the second number.

paragraphs.h3: Ajna’s physics sits on the calling-card ray

paragraphs: Physics O lies on the day ray: A — O — J — E. On the site point A is called the calling card: the first impression you make and your usual way of making contact. Point J is the step from an inner state to visible action. Our image: your way of working things out grows from the same root as your way of meeting people. The way you walk into a new group — straight in, cautiously, with a question, with a plan ready — is often the way you walk into a new task too.

sections.h2: Why The High Priestess never appears in the intuition chakra
paragraphs: The High Priestess is the great “intuitive” card of the tarot. Wen links her with inner knowing, intuition and hidden meaning. Yet she turns up in nobody’s Ajna, in any of the three columns. The Magician never appears there either.

The reason is arithmetic. Every Ajna number is the sum of two arcana: physics of the day and point J, energy of the month and point K, emotions of physics and energy. Here such sums are never less than four, and reducing the numbers from 23 to 44 gives 3 to 12. The numbers 1 and 2 have nowhere to come from.

The High Priestess lives one floor up, in Sahasrara. In Sahasrara’s physics she appears for people born on the 2nd of any month, in its energy for those born in February, and in its emotions only for those born on 1 January.

Waite gives this arithmetic some unexpected support. In the divinatory meanings of the Major Arcana he uses the word “intuition” once, and not for The High Priestess. Her list reads: “Secrets, mystery, the future as yet unrevealed… silence, tenacity; mystery, wisdom, science.” “Intuition” stands in the list for The Hanged Man: “Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy.” The Hanged Man does appear in Ajna, though rarely. In each of the three columns it is among the three rarest arcana, and in the Ajna row as a whole it turns up in roughly one calculation in twelve.

The most frequent arcanum in Ajna is The Hierophant. It comes first in both physics (8.7%) and energy (7.3%). Waite set it beside The High Priestess as her opposite: she is the hidden, inner side of a teaching, he is the open side, handed on through school and teacher. Frequency is a property of the calendar, not a verdict. But the picture is telling: in Ajna the matrix describes not knowledge out of nowhere but a path to understanding.

In his chapter on divination Waite himself writes that the value of intuition “is of course assumed”, and adds: “Where intuition fails, or is absent, concentration, intellectual observation and deduction must be used to the fullest extent… But intuition, even if apparently dormant, may be cultivated by practice.” And further: “it becomes possible with practice to distinguish between a guess of the conscious mind and an impression arising from the mind which is sub-conscious.” That is a good description of how Ajna works in the matrix. Its business is not miracles but telling things apart: a guess from knowledge, what was seen from what was filled in.
There are three cards where Waite speaks directly about sight. All three can appear in Ajna, in any column:

ul: **The Moon**: “The intellectual light is a reflection and beyond it is the unknown mystery which it cannot shew forth.”
**The Sun**: the light of consciousness here is “the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light”.
**Judgement**: “let those who have inward eyes look and discover therewith”.

paragraphs: Is there a Hanged Man, a Moon or a Hierophant in your Ajna? The calculator shows all three numbers in a second, along with the other six chakras.

sections.h2: Reading your Ajna: the meanings of arcana 3 to 22
paragraphs: Find each of your numbers in the right column. Under the name is the arcanum’s theme in Ajna, then how it sounds in each of the three roles. Every card has a side where it helps you understand and a side where it starts to get in the way. Both are given. Shares are calculated across all birth dates from 1940 to 2012.

In Waite, The Empress is “the outer sense of the Word”, but “she does not herself carry its interpretation”. The second, hidden sense of the Word is written on The High Priestess’s scroll. For Ajna this is a precise hint: the image is born easily, but it still has to be given a meaning.

ul: **Physics.** A thought grows gradually, out of observations and examples: a sketch, a mock-up, a living picture you can touch. You understand when you see an idea bear fruit. Shadow: growing a version so generously that it hurts to cut it back later.

**Energy.** Interest switches on at the chance to grow a design out of details and join observations into a living whole. Shadow: admiring the growth more than checking whether it is heading the right way.
**Emotions.** Joy when a thought sprouts and a whole harvest of ideas rises from a single guess. Shadow: disappointment when the harvest has to be thinned out for the sake of a result.

paragraphs.h3: 4 · The Emperor — understanding with a frame

paragraphs: Waite raises The Emperor to “the intellectual throne”, to “the lordship of thought”, and in the divinatory list names “reason, conviction”. The caveat is his too: this is not yet “the wisdom which draws from a higher world”. In Ajna’s energy and emotions The Emperor is the rarest arcanum (3.3% and 2.2%).

ul: **Physics.** A diagram, stages, key concepts: the frame first, then the details. With your explanation someone else can go through it step by step. Shadow: the diagram keeps growing until it mostly explains itself.

**Energy.** A need to understand how a thing is built and to know the limits of the question: interest holds while it is clear what belongs inside. Shadow: an awkward fact gets filed under “exceptions” and “I’ll sort it out later”.
**Emotions.** Confidence when everything is in its place. Shadow: irritation at facts that break a neat picture.

paragraphs.h3: 5 · The Hierophant — understanding through a school

paragraphs: The most frequent arcanum in Ajna: it turns up in 8.7% of calculations in physics and 7.3% in energy. Among the card’s meanings Waite lists “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”.

ul: **Physics.** Learning by a proven method, from a master, through a recognised programme, checking your thinking against the canon. Shadow: the authority of the source takes the place of understanding its argument.
**Energy.** A pull towards tested knowledge and a coherent teaching, a wish to belong to a school. Shadow: something new is accepted only once others have accepted it.
**Emotions.** Calm when an explanation is clear and shared with others. Shadow: confusion when two recognised systems contradict each other.

paragraphs: Wen sees in this card a choice in which heart and reason may fail to agree. In Ajna it becomes a way of understanding through comparison and agreement.

ul: **Physics.** You understand by comparing: two paths, the one chosen and the one turned down, an argument and what your heart tells you. Shadow: weighing things up forever so as not to choose.

**Energy.** Thinking together with someone close, opening your train of thought to each other. What you love is what you understand best. Shadow: checking your opinion against someone else’s until your own falls silent.
**Emotions.** Head and heart in agreement: the right answer feels like recognition. Shadow: awkwardness when your understanding parts ways with the choice of someone close.

paragraphs.h3: 7 · The Chariot — understanding on the move

paragraphs: Waite writes of “triumph in the mind”, but with a caveat: the liberation the charioteer brings “may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”.

ul: **Physics.** Testing an idea in action straight away, checking a version on the move and adjusting it along the way. Shadow: a conclusion before the task is understood.
**Energy.** The thrill of progress: whatever moves things forward is interesting. Shadow: dropping a question that gives no quick headway.
**Emotions.** The thrill of a move found and a puzzle cracked. Shadow: frustration when understanding requires standing still.

paragraphs.h3: 8 · Justice — understanding by a fair measure

paragraphs: The most frequent arcanum in Ajna’s emotions, at 8.5% of calculations. Waite’s divinatory list has “Equity, rightness, probity”. He himself made this card the eleventh, swapping it with Strength, though he admitted that Justice is “usually numbered eight”.

ul: **Physics.** Hearing both sides, weighing the inconvenient argument, looking for a refutation of your favourite version. Shadow: a trial instead of understanding.
**Energy.** A need for honest grounds and one measure for every argument. Shadow: demanding proof where there can be none.
**Emotions.** Relief at a fair outcome. Shadow: no peace until every side has been taken into account.

paragraphs.h3: 9 · The Hermit — understanding you reach yourself

paragraphs: The Hermit’s beacon, according to Waite, says “where I am, you also may be.” The light is held up so that others can see it.

ul: **Physics.** Working things out alone, in silence, step by step, testing them on yourself. Shadow: letting no one near your reasoning until it is ready.

**Energy.** A need to reach the heart of the matter yourself and understand it to the very bottom. Shadow: depth for its own sake, as the question sinks into navel-gazing while circumstances make the decision for you.
**Emotions.** The quiet joy of a conclusion of your own. Shadow: an understanding you never shared.

paragraphs.h3: 10 · The Wheel of Fortune — understanding repeats and turns

paragraphs: In Waite the sphinx on the Wheel stands for “stability amidst movement”. In Ajna this is the ability to see a pattern where others see chance.

ul: **Physics.** Noticing repeats and turning points, seeing events as a change of seasons, separating your own part from circumstances. Shadow: explaining everything with “that’s just how it turned out”.
**Energy.** Interest in the patterns inside change and in unexpected connections. Shadow: every piece of news stirs you up, and the picture never has time to settle.
**Emotions.** A lift at a turning point, joy at a connection found. Shadow: unease when the picture changes faster than you can make sense of it.

paragraphs: Waite rejects ordinary “self-confidence” as an explanation of this card: for him it is the higher nature, which tames the passions gently.

ul: **Physics.** Patiently working through the uncomfortable, calmly hearing out someone else’s argument, digging without accusing. Shadow: putting up with uncertainty longer than it deserves.
**Energy.** Gentle persistence: attention holds for a long time and doesn’t snap into a first reaction. Shadow: not letting go of a question it is time to drop.
**Emotions.** Calm in the face of a crack in the picture, confidence once it has been worked through. Shadow: keeping a straight face when you are in fact afraid of not understanding.

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man — understanding from the other side

paragraphs: The only card of the Major Arcana for which Waite names intuition among the divinatory meanings. The hanged man’s face, he says, expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”. In Ajna The Hanged Man is rare in every column: 2.4% in physics, 3.5% in energy, 2.5% in emotions.

ul: **Physics.** Turning the question over: looking at it from your opponent’s place, from a student’s, from the end of the road. Shadow: hanging over a question when it is time to act.
**Energy.** A readiness to give up a quick conclusion and step away from the question for a while. Shadow: “I’ll think about it some more” becomes a way of not deciding.
**Emotions.** Calmly staying with no answer. Shadow: getting so used to suspension that the answer is no longer needed.

paragraphs: Waite writes of the mystical death, entered while still in this life, as “a change in the form of consciousness”. Nothing could fit Ajna better. In physics it is the rarest arcanum: 2.25%.

ul: **Physics.** Closing down refuted models, honestly admitting that a version has had its day. Shadow: throwing out an explanation before it has been tested.
**Energy.** A readiness to relearn, a pull towards renewing what you know. Shadow: the new carries you off, and the old is left half thought through.
**Emotions.** Relief and sadness as you part with an earlier conclusion. Shadow: mourning for too long a version you put a lot into.

paragraphs.h3: 14 · Temperance — understanding blended from different sources

paragraphs: In Waite this card “tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures” of a person.

ul: **Physics.** Bringing sources together, stitching pieces of evidence, joining impressions with facts. Shadow: a compromise where a choice is needed.
**Energy.** Combining calculation with instinct and theory with practice, fitting the method to the task. Shadow: endless fine-tuning instead of a result.
**Emotions.** Evenness in the face of the unclear, a calm attitude to exceptions. Shadow: smoothing over a contradiction that deserved a closer look.

paragraphs.h3: 15 · The Devil — understanding that takes hold

paragraphs: On Waite’s card the chained figures have animal tails, “but there is human intelligence in the faces”. And the one above them is “not to be their master for ever”.

ul: **Physics.** Noticing what holds people: profit, weaknesses, the bait they fall for. Seeing the chains even at the top and noticing your own stake in a conclusion. Shadow: looking for a catch in everything.
**Energy.** Being gripped by a question: a thought you can’t tear yourself away from. Shadow: the thought starts to hold you.
**Emotions.** A strong attachment to your own version. Shadow: it is hard to give up a conclusion even when it has stopped explaining anything.

paragraphs.h3: 16 · The Tower — understanding that tests foundations

paragraphs: Waite sees in The Tower a ruin of the mind rather than of matter, “destruction on the intellectual side”: “the rending of a House of Doctrine… the reference is, however, to a House of Falsehood”.

ul: **Physics.** Checking the starting assumption, looking for the false support, testing an idea to breaking point. Shadow: breaking things before you have checked them.
**Energy.** The thrill of finding what everything rests on. Shadow: interest only where something is falling apart.
**Emotions.** A sudden insight, the shock of a mismatch. Shadow: after the jolt it is hard to trust even what is true.

paragraphs.h3: 17 · The Star — understanding that sees what is possible

paragraphs: Waite sees in the figure of The Star the Great Mother in the “supernal Understanding” of the Kabbalah, who gives to the spheres below “in the measure that they can receive her influx”. He links The High Priestess with the same supernal Understanding, but of these two cards only The Star ever appears in Ajna.

ul: **Physics.** Sketching the future, seeing a possibility that is not yet visible. Shadow: a beautiful image of the future instead of a check.
**Energy.** A pull towards prospects still out of sight, inspiration from generously shared knowledge. Shadow: hoping clarity will come by itself.
**Emotions.** Hope in the face of the unknown, inspiration from what is possible. Shadow: disappointment when reality turns out paler than the sketch.

paragraphs: For Waite The Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”. The path on the card leads into the unknown, and only reflected light shows the way.

ul: **Physics.** Catching shades, hints, things left unsaid. Telling what you saw from what you filled in. Shadow: filling it in.
**Energy.** The pull of mystery, a sensitivity to what is hidden. Shadow: the unclear attracts you more than the clear.
**Emotions.** A vague unease and an active imagination at the edge of the understood. Shadow: mistaking anxiety for intuition.

paragraphs.h3: 19 · The Sun — understanding in direct light

paragraphs: Waite explains the child on The Sun as “a child in the sense of simplicity and innocence in the sense of wisdom”.

ul: **Physics.** Putting the essence simply, showing it in daylight, with no dark corners. Shadow: simplifying until it is no longer true.
**Energy.** A wish to see the whole picture clearly, for yourself and for others. Shadow: a dislike of questions that have no simple answer.
**Emotions.** Joy at a simple, clear answer. In this column The Sun is uncommon: 2.8%. Shadow: impatience with the half-dark you sometimes have to walk through.

paragraphs.h3: 20 · Judgement — understanding what you have lived through

paragraphs: Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response — almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?”

ul: **Physics.** Reviewing the road behind you, looking back honestly, gathering all the evidence. Shadow: reviewing the past without end.
**Energy.** Interest in where it all led, the call of lived experience. Shadow: searching the past for an answer about the future.
**Emotions.** Clarity as an awakening, an inner “this is it”. Shadow: the insight demands an immediate response and leaves no time to check it.

paragraphs: Waite’s World is “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”. In Ajna it is the need to see how all the parts fit together.

ul: **Physics.** Holding the whole system in mind, bringing different sides into one picture. Shadow: the picture matters more than the details that don’t fit it.
**Energy.** A need to grasp how the whole is built. Shadow: not starting until you can see all of it.
**Emotions.** Joy at a whole that has come together. Shadow: in time a neat system starts explaining yesterday.

paragraphs: Waite’s Fool has a face “full of intelligence and expectant dream”. This is not foolishness but “the spirit in search of experience”.

ul: **Physics.** Taking on the unfamiliar as a beginner, testing by trying rather than by arguing, asking about the simplest things. Shadow: giving up at the trial stage.
**Energy.** Freedom from “that’s how it has always been done” and “I already know what he’s like”. Shadow: doubting everything and asserting nothing.
**Emotions.** Lightness in the face of the unfamiliar, the joy of not knowing. Shadow: the beginner’s position as a hiding place, with the conclusion put off again and again.

paragraphs: The table of meanings gives you words, but not the meaning of a row. The Hanged Man in physics next to The Wheel in energy means one thing; next to The Moon, something quite different. You can see how in the examples below.

sections.h2: Ajna’s special rows
paragraphs: **One card in two columns.** Physics matches energy in 20 rows, from 3-3-6 to 22-22-8. This happens slightly more often than once in twelve calculations. It is not a doubling of the quality. In energy the card describes what makes you want to work something out, in physics how you go about it. For these people the way they think coincides with what they like to think about, so what they feel at the edge of the understood matters all the more. This is how it sounds in the full reading for row 4-4-8: “The Emperor appears here twice, and he works differently each time. In the way you handle information he is a method: gather the facts, put each one in its place, see what follows from what. In your energy he becomes a motive — you are fed by the right to bring order to your understanding yourself, rather than accept someone else’s ready-made conclusion. Justice shapes how clarity feels: a conclusion satisfies you when everything has been honestly taken into account, including the inconvenient parts.”

**Mirror rows and The Moon.** Add 18 to any number from 5 to 11, reduce the sum, and you get the same number back: 7 + 18 = 25 → 7. That is why Ajna has twelve rows where emotions repeat the neighbouring card. These are X-18-X, with The Moon in energy, and 18-X-X, with The Moon in physics. Such a row falls to about one date in 27. In Waite The Moon is the card of reflected light, and in arithmetic it behaves the same way: it reflects the number beside it. Our reading: for these people the feeling at the edge of the understood is a reflection of their way of working things out, or of their interest, seen in half-light.

**The most and the least common.** Ajna has 336 possible rows in all. Across all dates from 1940 to 2012, the most common is 10-10-20, about once in 117 dates. Next come 11-11-22, 9-11-20, 8-10-18 and 11-9-20. At the other end are the one-offs:

ul: **4-22-8** falls to a single date in two hundred years, from 1900 to 2100: 18 September 2000. That date’s year arcanum is 2, and in these two centuries only the year 2000 has that digit sum.
**21-14-8** and **20-9-11** last appeared in 1940, on 18 January and 17 July, and will not return until 2039. Nobody born between 1941 and 2038 has them.
**20-21-5** appeared on 17 April 1943, 1952, 1961 and 1970, and will next appear in 2069.

paragraphs: Even 4-22-8 has its own text in the full reading. It is called “Curiosity that carries a map”.

sections.h2: Reading your row: 12 / 10 / 22 worked through
paragraphs: Take the same date, 31.03.1993. The Ajna row is The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune, The Fool.

ol: **Energy — The Wheel of Fortune.** Interest is switched on by change: what has shifted, what keeps repeating, where a turn has come.

**Physics — The Hanged Man.** Working things out here means stopping and looking from the other side. In Waite the tree the man hangs from is “living wood”, and his face expresses absorption, not torment.
**Emotions — The Fool.** At the edge of the understood there is lightness: you may not yet know how it all works and still give it a try.
**One connecting thought.** When the old answer stops working, you are able to see a different move.

paragraphs: This is how the row looks in the full reading:
**Finding a way out where there was a dead end**

head: Position

rows: Seeing it from the other side

paragraphs: Sometimes a solution comes into view only after you stop pushing for the old answer. In Ajna, the chakra of mind and understanding, The Hanged Man brings this kind of pause: the habitual view loosens its grip for a while. The Wheel of Fortune reminds you that circumstances may already have changed. And The Fool lets you meet the unfamiliar with curiosity — not yet knowing how it all works, and still trying to figure it out. **Your opportunity here is to see a different move.** Say a piece of work stalls at the same stage time after time. At first you just want to push harder. But a look from the outside reveals something else: the people involved each understand the result differently. So instead of yet another push, a clear agreement appears. The understanding of the task itself changes — and what seemed impossible to get past finally gives way. The flip side is falling in love with a new explanation too quickly. A moment ago everything seemed clear, but then something else happened — and the old picture fell apart. The next version is just as captivating, and you want to start over. If no idea has time to meet experience, thinking turns into one endless house move: every place is interesting, none is lived in. Clarity comes when a new view is carried on into action.

Notice where the difficulty came from. It is not in any of the cards on its own. The Hanged Man can let go of the old view, The Wheel notices that everything has already changed, The Fool happily starts again. All three pull towards a new explanation, and none of them holds on to the old one long enough to test it in action.

paragraphs.h3: One energy, four ways of understanding

paragraphs: The Moon turns up in Ajna’s energy in roughly one calculation in twenty. It is a pull towards the unsaid and the hidden. But what a person with that pull actually does is decided by the neighbouring cards.

head: Date
