rows: Solving a mystery by your own light
Within a legend, you can make out what really happened.
Turning a hunch into knowledge with a trial step
With a small test you turn a hunch into knowledge.
Your hunches can be trusted because you check them.
Grasp the complex through an unexpected image
What puzzles you becomes yours once you find the image it lives in.

paragraphs: The Hermit follows the unclear alone, by his own lantern, until he reaches the bottom. The Fool doesn’t guess but takes a small step and watches what happens, while The Emperor in emotions brings calm once the mystery has a firm outline. Strength tests a hunch with a calm question, and uncertainty doesn’t frighten it. The Hanged Man shifts the angle, and the puzzle opens up through an image from which, as with The Empress, a harvest of ideas grows. The same Moon, four different minds. That is why the reading of a single arcanum can never replace the reading of a row.

sections.h2: Your Ajna and the other six chakras
paragraphs: Seven chakras, three arcana in each: physics, energy, emotions. The numbers appear straight after the free calculation. The interpretations open in the full reading; until you pay, the rows are locked.

Ajna is one row out of seven, and it has the closest ties to its neighbours. Its physics and energy are built from Sahasrara and Vishuddha, and its energy also stands in the middle of the talent line. In the matrix, understanding does not live on its own: it grows out of what matters to you and is tested by what you can put into words.
The full chakra reading for your date contains:

ul: **seven sections, from Muladhara to Sahasrara**, each with its own title, main idea and captions for the three arcana: the role each card plays in that chakra;

**three connected paragraphs per chakra**: the chakra’s theme and what each card brings to it, a picture of how the combination looks in life, and the difficulty that grows out of the same combination;

**a separate text for each of Ajna’s 336 possible rows**: not three dictionary meanings glued together, but a reading of that exact combination, including the row that fell to a single date in two hundred years;
**a summary, “What matters most for you”**: the thread that ties the seven chakras into one portrait, and the main tension in your chart.

sections.h2: “Opening the third eye”: what Ajna really shows
paragraphs: A great deal is written about the third eye: how to “open” it, the signs that it is “closed”, which numbers give “strong intuition”. The destiny matrix cannot be read that way.

ul: **The numbers are names of arcana, not scores.** 22 is not stronger than 3, The Moon does not make anyone clairvoyant, and The Emperor does not block intuition. There is no such thing as an empty Ajna: everyone has three cards in it.
**“Plus” and “minus” are not different arcana but two modes of the same one.** Your way of understanding and its typical trap grow from one root. The trap begins where a strength goes too far.

head: Strong side
What it turns into when it goes too far
rows: The Emperor: building a clear diagram
The Hierophant: learning from what is proven
someone else’s authority instead of your own understanding
The Chariot: testing an idea in action straight away
a conclusion before the task is understood
The Hermit: working it out yourself
letting no one near your reasoning
The Devil: being gripped by a question
a thought that won’t let go
The Tower: finding the false foundation
imagination fills in what isn’t there
The Fool: looking as a beginner
an endless “I’m still figuring it out”, and no conclusion

paragraphs: So instead of “how do I open my Ajna?” it is more useful to ask: where does my way of understanding slip into its shadow? In the full reading the third paragraph of every chakra is about exactly that shift, and it is written for your combination, not for the arcanum in general.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation**: Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, J = A + E, K = B + E, Ajna’s physics O = A + J, energy P = B + K, emotions = O + P. Every sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All the numerical facts — the 336 possible rows, the absence of 1 and 2, the match between energy and the talent line, the frequencies of arcana and rows, the single date for row 4-22-8 — come from running through every date from 1900 to 2100. Shares are given for all birth dates from 1940 to 2012.

**Card meanings**: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), including the divinatory meanings and the chapter on divination in Part III, and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), the chapter on the Seven Chakras spread. Quotations are given in the authors’ original English.
**Tradition**: the Shat-chakra-nirupana in Arthur Avalon’s translation (The Serpent Power, 1919), verses 32–33 with commentary.

Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix. The physics / energy / emotions columns, the meanings of the arcana in Ajna, and the links with Sahasrara, Vishuddha and the talent line are the author’s interpretation.

This is a symbolic model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a medical description. The numbers say nothing about intelligence, eyesight, physical condition or supernatural abilities, and they do not decide whether anyone’s chakras are “open”.

paragraphs: **Find out how clarity comes to you.** Enter your date of birth and you will see the three arcana of your Ajna and of the other six chakras straight away. In the full reading each of the seven chakras is read as a whole: what matters to you, how it looks in life, and where a strength turns into a trap.

faq.q: Where is Ajna in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In the upper-left sector of the diagram. Physics is point O on the day ray, second from the edge, between the birth day A and point J. Energy is point P on the month ray, also second from the edge, between the month B and point K. Emotions are their sum and have no point of their own on the diagram. In our table Ajna is the sixth row, between Vishuddha and Sahasrara.

faq.q: How do I calculate Ajna from my date of birth?
faq.a: You need the day arcanum A, the month B and the year arcanum C, which is the sum of the year’s digits. Work out D = A + B + C and the centre E = A + B + C + D. Then J = A + E and K = B + E. Physics = A + J, energy = B + K, emotions = physics + energy. Anything above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. For 31.03.1993, for example, you get 12 / 10 / 22.

faq.q: I have The Moon or The Hanged Man in Ajna. Does that mean strong intuition?
faq.a: No, and the opposite does not follow either. The Moon describes a sensitivity to the unsaid and to images at the edge of the understood, which still have to be told apart from guesses. The Hanged Man is a way of understanding by changing the angle. Waite names intuition only among The Hanged Man’s meanings, but even that card is no measure of a gift. How far your guesses turn into understanding is shown by the whole row, not by a single card.

faq.q: Why do The High Priestess and The Magician never appear in Ajna?
faq.a: Because of arithmetic. Every Ajna number is the sum of two arcana, and here that sum is never less than four. Reducing the numbers from 23 to 44 gives 3 to 12. So 1 and 2 never come up in anyone’s Ajna. The High Priestess appears one floor up, in Sahasrara: for people born on the 2nd of a month, in February or on 1 January.

faq.q: Are Ajna’s energy and the talent line the same thing?
faq.a: The number is the same: Ajna’s energy always equals the middle number of the talent line B–P–K, because both come from point P. But the roles differ. In the talent line P shows the form in which your gift unfolds. In Ajna it shows what switches on your interest in understanding. The match means that what you are curious to understand and how your gift unfolds are described by one and the same card.

faq.q: How can I tell if my Ajna is “closed”?
faq.a: Not from the numbers. An arcanum’s number is the name of a symbol, not a score, and everyone has all three columns filled. What popular readings call a “closed” Ajna is usually one of three failures: I can’t get into it, I keep going round in circles, I understand but don’t trust myself. It is more useful to find out which column your chain breaks on.

faq.q: Is Ajna different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, so a man and a woman born on the same date have the same numbers. Nor does the reading split understanding into “female intuition” and “male logic”: any card can appear in anyone’s Ajna.

faq.q: Can I change my Ajna?
faq.a: The numbers don’t change: they come from your date of birth. What changes is how you use them. The Emperor can build a diagram that explains the task, or defend the diagram against the task. The Moon can hear what is left unsaid, or fill it in. The Fool can ask the question that shifts everything, or hide in not knowing. The row shows both the trap and the strength of one and the same way of understanding.

items.title: Vishuddha
level: Vishuddha is in charge of the word, and of the fate that builds up out of what gets said. Everything to do with honesty lands here: whether a person keeps promises, calls things by their names, can say “no” without three days of preparation.

This level shows up most clearly in career and reputation. A strong Vishuddha gives a voice people believe and the timing to say the right thing; a blocked one gives a lump in the throat, an endless “I will keep quiet, it will sort itself out”, and grudges nobody but their owner knows about.
items.personal_intro: Speaking and listening: how you express an idea, why you start a conversation and how you feel about the response.

columns.title: Physics
columns.text: The work where a voice turns into a result: negotiations, texts, teaching, sales. The column also shows whether a person is paid for what they say and write.

columns.title: Energy
columns.text: Puts drive into a conversation and carries the weight of someone else’s pressure without snapping and without going silent. An empty column: the voice gives out exactly when it is time to answer.

columns.title: Emotions
columns.text: Honesty with yourself lives here. At its best a person says what they think and is calm once the talk is over; at its worst they store up the unsaid, then pour it all out at once and at the wrong person.

article.short: Vishuddha in the destiny matrix is the fifth chakra. On our energy map it comes straight after Anahata: from closeness to the word. Its theme is speech and influence. The three numbers of the row answer three questions: how you speak, what you enter a conversation for, and what happens inside you when the answer comes. Physics is the chart’s inner left point J (the day arcanum plus the centre), energy is the inner point of talent K (the month plus the centre), and emotions are their sum.

intro: Your Vishuddha is the fifth row of the table. Enter your date of birth to see your three arcana.

sections.h2: Finding your Vishuddha from your date of birth
paragraphs: You need five numbers from the matrix and three more additions. One rule holds for the whole calculation: if a sum is greater than 22, add up its digits (29 → 11, 40 → 4), and keep going until you get a number from 1 to 22.
Take 31 March 1993 as an example.

ol: **A, the day arcanum:** 31 → 3 + 1 = 4.
**B, the month:** 3.
**C, the year arcanum:** 1 + 9 + 9 + 3 = 22.
**Vishuddha physics:** A + E = 4 + 4 = **8**, Justice.
**Vishuddha energy:** B + E = 3 + 4 = **7**, the Chariot.
**Vishuddha emotions:** 8 + 7 = **15**, the Devil.

paragraphs: If you already know the centre of your matrix, it is simpler still: Vishuddha is “day plus centre” and “month plus centre”. In the calculator the whole table of seven chakras appears as soon as you enter a date — free and with no sign-up.

On the matrix diagram these two numbers sit on the left and top rays, in the third of five points counting from the edge towards the centre. Other guides put it as “one point on the horizontal line, the other on the vertical” — they mean the same cells, J and K.

sections.h2: Why Vishuddha is called the throat of the matrix
paragraphs: The throat is the narrow passage between head and heart: thought and feeling have to pass through it to become words. In the destiny matrix this is not a metaphor but the order of the calculation. The left and top rays of the chart each carry five points from the edge to the centre, and the chakras take them in turn: Sahasrara on the edge, then Ajna, Vishuddha and Anahata, with Manipura at the centre.

Vishuddha’s numbers are worked out before its neighbours’, straight from the edge of the chart and its centre. Only then do they give Ajna (edge plus Vishuddha) and Anahata (Vishuddha plus centre). The head and the heart of the matrix cannot be calculated without the throat.
The same calculation shows what your voice is made of.

**Physics: the calling card the centre speaks through.** J = A + E. In the matrix the day arcanum is the calling card: the first impression and your usual way of making contact. The centre is your main inner state, the comfort zone. Vishuddha’s physics joins the two: this is how you sound when there was no time to prepare a role and you speak as you are. It is easiest to hear in a heated argument, in answer to an unexpected question, in the first sentence after a pause. In the “Karmic task before 40” section of the reading, the same point J is read as your habitual way of matching the image you show with your inner footing.
**Energy: talent on its way out.** K = B + E, and it is the last point of the talent line. The line itself runs down the energy column of the three upper chakras:

Energy

rows: the form of work that suits it
**what the gift becomes once it has matured**

paragraphs: Talent comes down from above, from idea to form, and goes out to people through the throat. Vishuddha’s energy is ability in its finished state: no longer something to show off or prove, just something you calmly use. That is why the question “what do you speak up for?” almost coincides here with “what is your gift?”. The Hierophant in energy wants to pass on knowledge, the Star to give back hope, the World to translate some people into the language of others. When your work lets you speak for that, the words come easily. When it does not, being tired of talking often turns out to be tiredness with someone else’s goal.

**The centre sounds in both numbers.** E goes into J and into K alike. And the centre of the matrix is also Manipura, the chakra of will. In this system the voice grows from the same place as the will: what is inside is what comes out in words.

**Its mirror pair is Svadhisthana.** The matrix has four inner points. The left and top ones, J and K, go to Vishuddha; the right and bottom ones, L and M, go to Svadhisthana, the chakra of desire and pleasure. One wants, the other speaks: two halves of one inner square.

sections.h2: Vishuddha in tradition: sixteen vowels and the white moon of ether
paragraphs: The chakra’s name comes from the Sanskrit viśuddha, “especially pure”. The best-known old description is in Purnananda’s treatise Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577), which English readers know from John Woodroffe’s translation in The Serpent Power (1919). There Vishuddha looks like this:

ul: a lotus in the throat, “of a smoky purple hue”;
sixteen petals, each carrying one of the sixteen vowels of Sanskrit;
in the middle, a circular region of ether, akasha, “white like the full Moon”;
the chakra’s syllable is HAM, seated on an elephant “white as snow”;
of the one who has mastered this chakra, the text says that he becomes “eloquent and wise”.

paragraphs: The detail about the vowels is one to remember. A consonant gives a word its shape, but a vowel can be drawn out by the voice — the sound rests on it. The petals of the throat carry the voice of the alphabet. Ether was not chosen by chance either: in Indian philosophy its quality is sound. The blue that Vishuddha is painted in today came much later, in Western books of the 20th century, where the chakras were given the colours of the rainbow.

In Benebell Wen’s Holistic Tarot (2015), card 5 of the Seven Chakras Spread corresponds with the throat chakra and “denotes expression, community, and communication”. From this card she reads “how the Seeker expresses his or her views” and “the Seeker’s relationship to others and how the Seeker expresses or communicates that relationship”. The destiny matrix is not a spread: instead of one drawn card we have three calculated arcana, each with a question of its own. But the question of the fifth chakra is the same — what happens when what is inside gets said.

sections.h2: Vishuddha’s three columns: how you speak, why, and what you feel
paragraphs: The columns of the energy map have the same names in every row — physics, energy, emotions. But in each chakra they ask a question of their own. In Vishuddha it goes like this.

**Physics is delivery.** How a thought turns into words: directly or gently, briefly or with examples, through facts or through images. It is what the other person hears before they have even grasped the meaning. The test question: how do I talk when there is no time to choose my words?

**Energy is motive.** Why you start talking at all: to reach a decision, to keep someone close, to pass on knowledge, to name the truth, to make people laugh. The same calm tone can serve different ends, and sooner or later the other person senses which one. The question: what do I want from this conversation?

**Emotions are the response.** What the answer does to you: pleases, stings, calms, will not let go. Emotions are the sum of the first two numbers, and in life you can see it plainly: how you take an answer grows out of how you spoke and what for. Whoever wanted a decision waits for a “yes”. Whoever wanted to be understood waits for recognition. The question: what do I feel when the other person answers — or says nothing?
The arcana that come up most often in the emotions column are the Hierophant, the Lovers and the Chariot — each at about 9% of dates. The rarest is Death: about 1%.

The main rule of reading: three numbers make one scene, not three separate traits. The row 8 / 7 / 15 is not “honesty, drive and dependence”. It is a person who weighs every word, steers an argument to a clear agreement and then cannot let go of someone else’s “no” for a long time. How numbers add up to a scene like this is shown after the reference.

sections.h2: The arcana in Vishuddha: meanings from 3 to 22
paragraphs: Find your three numbers and read the lines you need: physics for the first number, energy for the second, emotions for the third. “Where it goes wrong” describes how the strength of the arcanum starts to get in the way of a conversation. It is a possible scenario, not a verdict.
The Magician (1) and the High Priestess (2) never appear in any column of Vishuddha. The reason is in the questions at the end of the article.

ul: **Physics.** Warm, vivid speech: an example instead of a rule, support before advice. People feel calmer after talking to you. In physics the Empress is rare — about 2% of dates.

**Energy.** The wish for something to grow out of the conversation: a person’s confidence, an idea, a shared project. The rarest energy in Vishuddha: across the years 1900–2099 it goes to one single date — 1 August 2000.
**Emotions.** Warmth when a word takes root: the advice came in useful, the person blossomed, came back with a result.
**Where it goes wrong.** Care starts deciding for the other person what it is time for them to know. An unpleasant truth is softened beyond recognition, and the other person gets a filtered picture.
**Physics.** Speaking point by point: terms, deadlines, who is responsible for what. After a conversation with you it is clear what to do next. Rare — about 2% of dates.
**Energy.** To bring order and share out responsibility: everyone gets their part of the job, your own people get protection. A rare energy, about 0.6% of dates.
**Emotions.** The calm of certainty: there is a frame, the roles are clear. What unsettles you is agreements starting to drift.
**Where it goes wrong.** Discussion turns into handing out orders. A rule has to be explained again, and irritation grows faster than understanding.
**Physics.** Explaining what everything rests on: why things are done this way, what has been tested, what the lesson is. You speak a shared language, and people trust you.

**Energy.** To pass on knowledge: to teach, to make someone else’s experience understandable, to keep the meaning of what is passing away. Among the meanings of this card Waite lists “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”.

**Emotions.** Satisfaction when you were understood and the advice came in useful; your footing is the agreement of your own circle. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s emotions, almost 10% of dates.
**Where it goes wrong.** Advice starts to sound compulsory. If it is not taken, it hurts as if you yourself had been rejected — and teaching quietly turns into lecturing.
**Physics.** Speaking as a partner: as equals, one to one, without masks. Your words are fair to both of you.
**Energy.** To come to an agreement and stay on the same side. You need the conversation for the bond, not for the win.
**Emotions.** The joy of a match: a mutual “yes”, making up after a falling-out.
**Where it goes wrong.** Any disagreement feels like a threat to the relationship. A convenient “yes” is said for the sake of peace, and the real “no” piles up until the first quarrel.
**Physics.** Speech that leads to a goal: short, direct, with a clear next step. You know how to steer a discussion to an outcome.
**Energy.** To get a question moving: to bring the conversation to a decision, to close what has dragged on.
**Emotions.** The thrill of moving forward and the triumph of a “yes”.

**Where it goes wrong.** The other person has not yet understood the task, and you are already at the next turn. A pause feels like defeat, the conversation becomes a race, and the agreement is wrung out rather than shared.
**Physics.** Precision: facts without exaggeration, terms without guile, a claim kept apart from a guess.
**Energy.** To speak honestly and to the point, so that everything falls into place for both sides.
**Emotions.** Relief when the conversation ends in an honest result.

**Where it goes wrong.** Precision turns into a trial: who is right, who is to blame, where the other person put it inaccurately. The record is flawless, and the person opposite feels like the accused.
**Physics.** Precision in few words. You speak when the thought is thought through, and you can listen without interrupting.

**Energy.** First to work it out for yourself, then to share what you found. Waite describes the Hermit’s lantern as a beacon that says “where I am, you also may be”. In Vishuddha this is the wish to light the way for someone else with what you have been through yourself.
**Emotions.** A deep, unhurried response: an answer needs to ripen in private.

**Where it goes wrong.** The pause drags on, the other person does not know what you think and decides for you. What you left unsaid seems obvious to you — and it surprises you that nobody understood it.
**Physics.** A sense of the moment: your words adjust to a new turn, and you know when to speak up.
**Energy.** An interest in live exchange — in the unexpected question and in where the talk will turn.
**Emotions.** A lift from the twists of a conversation — and a swing: hope, doubt, hope again.
**Where it goes wrong.** Your position shifts with the mood of the conversation. A promise made on one turn is forgotten on the next, and people struggle to tell which of your words they can rely on.

**Physics.** Firmness without pressure: calmly holding your ground and saying “no” without raising your voice. On Waite’s card a woman gently closes a lion’s mouth — for the throat chakra the image is almost literal. Waite even noted that in the earlier form of the card “she is obviously opening it”, and judged the closing gesture “better symbolically”. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s physics — almost 7% of dates.
**Energy.** To withstand someone else’s pressure and not drop your thought: soft steadiness instead of a counter-blow.
**Emotions.** A strong response you manage to hold: the wave rises — and becomes a boundary, not an attack.
**Where it goes wrong.** Restraint builds up until it flares, or sets into stubbornness: “I am calm, but I will not move an inch.”
**Physics.** Hearing someone out and checking back: saying how you understood them, looking at the question from the other side.
**Energy.** To understand someone else’s truth, putting your ready answer aside.
**Emotions.** Sympathy for the other person’s side, and a pause after which the answer looks different.
**Where it goes wrong.** In conversation there is only ever room for someone else’s story. Your own answer stays outside the door, and a quiet resentment builds up that nobody knows about.
**Physics.** Ending clearly: putting a full stop, speaking plainly about a change, closing an argument that has run its course.
**Energy.** To let go of what has outlived itself: a role, a formula, familiar phrases that no longer work.
**Emotions.** Living through an ending — with sadness and with the relief of final clarity. The rarest arcanum in Vishuddha’s emotions, about 1% of dates.
**Where it goes wrong.** The full stop comes abruptly and without explanation. Or it never comes at all, and a conversation that ended long ago drags on out of fear of saying “that’s it”.
**Physics.** A soft, even tone and carefully chosen words: unhurried, but clear.

**Energy.** To join different positions and find a third way. Waite writes that the rule of this card “tempers, combines and harmonises” the psychic and material natures. In Vishuddha this is the wish to bring the incompatible together in one conversation. One of the most common energies, about 7.5% of dates.
**Emotions.** Taking any answer evenly and quickly getting your balance back.
**Where it goes wrong.** For the sake of peace, the very difference the decision depends on gets smoothed over. Everything is agreed, everyone is happy — and the main thing is never named.
**Physics.** Speaking plainly about what is wanted: naming the gain, the interest, the temptation — what people usually keep quiet about. Your speech is magnetic and persuasive.
**Energy.** A strong wish to influence, to carry people along, to get your way. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s energy, about 7.6% of dates.
**Emotions.** Attachment to the answer: pleasure when your words worked, and a tight grip when you were refused.

**Where it goes wrong.** Self-interest hides behind “I’m only advising”, influence turns into hidden pressure, and a refusal into defeat. An interest named out loud stops tugging at the conversation in secret.
**Physics.** Saying out loud what everyone walks around: a broken promise, the gap between words and deeds, pretence.

**Energy.** To stop playing at order and bring down a facade held up by things left unsaid. Among the old titles of this card Waite gives “the Tower of Babel”, and he calls it “assuredly a card of confusion”. Babel is the story of how people stopped understanding each other. The Tower in Vishuddha wants people to understand each other for real, even at the cost of a collapse.
**Emotions.** A sharp reaction to falseness: a flare-up when words never became deeds.
**Where it goes wrong.** The truth sounds like a verdict on the person rather than a statement of fact. The blow brings relief, but afterwards there is nobody left to talk to.
**Physics.** Vivid speech, a story, support for someone else’s plan: you speak so that a person sees what is possible.
**Energy.** To pass on hope — to bring back the belief that it will work out.
**Emotions.** Inspiration from a response, joy in someone else’s hope.
**Where it goes wrong.** A beautiful image runs ahead of what you are ready to do. And if the other person does not share your picture of the future, the disappointment is stronger than any argument.
**Physics.** Carefully finding words for something hazy: asking back, separating what was heard from what only seemed to be said.
**Energy.** To hear what lies under the words: tone, pauses, what is left unsaid.
**Emotions.** Sensitivity to half-tones — and anxiety when the answer is unclear or the other person goes quiet.
**Where it goes wrong.** A guess about a hidden meaning is taken for fact. An inner dialogue for two replaces one simple question: “Is that what you meant?”
**Physics.** Openly, simply and in front of everyone: saying what you want, acknowledging someone else’s success, voicing a thought with no hidden agenda.
**Energy.** To share what delights you and lights you up — and to be heard.
**Emotions.** Joy when you are understood: that very “got it!” in the other person’s eyes.
**Where it goes wrong.** Performing crowds out conversation, and there is no room left for anyone else’s answer. A calm reaction from listeners hurts like coldness.
**Physics.** Saying your piece about what matters: naming a decision that is overdue, summing up, calling for reconciliation.

**Energy.** To answer an inner call and speak about what has lasting meaning. On this card everything begins with a sound: the angel blows the trumpet, and the dead rise. Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response—almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?”
**Emotions.** Relief when the important thing is finally named; someone else’s answer comes as an awakening.

**Where it goes wrong.** Every conversation becomes a trial of the past. Or the other way round: your own voice drowns in familiar family judgements, and having an opinion of your own feels like betrayal.
**Physics.** Translating from one language to another: explaining some people to others, finding words for every circle — different professions, generations, views.
**Energy.** To gather everyone into a shared meaning, so that nobody is left out.
**Emotions.** Satisfaction when the whole picture comes together and different people understand each other.
**Where it goes wrong.** Talk about the whole hides the specifics: the big picture is drawn, but who does what by Friday is never said.
**Physics.** A simple question out loud, a joke, trying out a phrasing on the fly — speech without armour.
**Energy.** Conversation without a script: curiosity about the other person, the courage not to know the answer in advance.
**Emotions.** Lightness before any answer, even a refusal.
**Where it goes wrong.** A joke stands in for an answer. Being asked to make clear where the joke ends and the promise begins feels like an attack on your freedom.

sections.h2: Why three meanings from a reference are not yet a reading
paragraphs: A reference says what each arcanum does on its own. In a living person the arcana do not just stand side by side — they change one another. Here is the Devil, for many the most alarming card, in six different Vishuddhas. On the right are the titles and key thoughts of the interpretations in the full reading.

rows: “Words that bind people to a promise”
After your message, a vague “later” becomes a commitment that gets kept.
Your “why not?” can thaw someone who has long lived on nothing but “I have to”.
You can stay close to strong tension without letting it control your words.
“Helping a loved one believe in themselves again”
In your words, a person sees themselves as strong again.
“Steering a conversation to a clear decision”

paragraphs: One arcanum, six different people. Next to Justice and the Chariot, the Devil becomes someone else’s answer that holds on longer than the conversation itself. Next to Temperance and Strength, it is a pull towards a sharp exchange you can hardly tear yourself away from. Next to the Star, a stubborn wish to help someone close believe in themselves. Paired with itself, a gift for talking a person into joy. From the dictionary’s “temptation and dependence” you cannot get to a single one of these pictures.

That is why the full reading has no dictionary. A separate text has been written for each of the 379 combinations that occur among people born from 1900 to 2099. It has three parts: what your Vishuddha is about, how the combination looks in life, and where it starts to get in the way.

paragraphs: Your speech carries the scales and sword of Justice: your words are weighed, and what you say cuts through confusion. You call things by their names, hear both sides out and even say no with your reasons attached. It is the Chariot that draws you into a conversation: talking is a journey with a destination, and you want to steer it past every objection to an outcome. And the other person’s reply goes deep — that is the Devil of your Vishuddha: someone else’s “yes” or “no” can hold you longer than the conversation itself lasted.

The group chat has spent three days arguing over who pays what for a trip together. The messages multiply, and so do the grievances. You write one message: who takes on what, why that’s fair and the date to settle it all by. **You can turn an argument into an agreement where everyone knows what they have signed up to.** The thread ends in a to-do list rather than a row, and the others’ agreement grips you like a small victory you keep wanting to relive.

But what if a well-weighed argument is turned down? The reasoning is fair, the road to the goal is clear — and the answer is still “no”. The Chariot doesn’t like standing still, and the conversation easily turns into a contest where the point is no longer to agree but to be proven right. Someone else’s refusal holds you like a chain: in the evening you replay the conversation, find new arguments, read motives into their words that may never have been there. A solution may well be found, but trust gets left somewhere halfway down the road.

Compare this with what a reference would give you: “honesty, drive, attachment”. All true, but the scene — a person who ends a three-day argument with one message and in the evening replays someone else’s “no” — is nowhere in those words.

sections.h2: A “blocked Vishuddha”: what the numbers really show
paragraphs: Popular articles on chakras carry lists of “signs of a blocked Vishuddha”, from a fear of speaking in public to the proverbial lump in the throat. The numbers of the matrix show nothing of the kind. An arcanum is a symbol, not a score. Every cell of the table is filled, and there is no number that would mean “the chakra is blocked” or “in the minus”. The Devil in emotions is no worse than the Sun, and Death in physics is no more dangerous than the Empress.
What the numbers do show is something else: where a conversation can break down. When Vishuddha falters, the trouble almost always sits in one of the three columns.

head: Where it broke
What it looks like
Which number to read
rows: it came out harsher, softer or longer than you meant; the right thought sounded wrong
the conversation began for the sake of a decision and went on for the sake of being right, of quiet or of approval
after someone else’s “no” there is nothing left to say; the other person’s silence is louder than their words

paragraphs: How to find where yours falters. Recall a recent conversation that left you feeling “they didn’t hear me”. Reconstruct what was actually said — the words themselves, not their meaning. Work out where it broke: in the words, in the goal or in how you took the answer. Then read “Where it goes wrong” for the arcanum in that column. Most often what you find there is not someone else’s fault but your own strength, which overdid it this time.

sections.h2: Common mistakes in reading Vishuddha

ul: **Reading the number as a grade.** 22 is not “stronger” than 3, and 15 is not “more dangerous” than 6. The number is the name of a symbol, not an amount of energy.

**Taking the general meaning of the arcanum instead of its column.** The Devil in Vishuddha’s emotions is not “dependence in general” but attachment to the other person’s answer. The Chariot in physics is not “travel” but speech that leads to a goal.
**Gluing three meanings into a list.** “Honest, driven, dependent” is three dictionary entries, not a person. The reading begins when a single scene comes into view.

**Carrying names over from another system.** The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. In Waite’s deck and in many tarot books these two cards trade places — Waite himself wrote that he made the swap “for reasons which satisfy myself”. The meaning rests on the name of the card: in someone else’s reference, look up not the number but Justice or Strength.
**Looking for a forecast in Vishuddha.** The row describes your way of speaking, your motive and your response. It says nothing about events — who will say what, how an argument will end.

sections.h2: See your own Vishuddha
paragraphs: The matrix calculation is free and needs no sign-up. As soon as you enter a date you see the whole “Chakras and your arcana” table: seven rows, three arcana in each. Vishuddha is the fifth row of our table.

The interpretation opens in the full reading. There each chakra has a section of its own, as in the 8 / 7 / 15 example: the name of the combination, captions for the three arcana and a connected text — what this chakra is about for you, how the combination looks in life and where it starts to get in the way. All 379 variants of Vishuddha are written this way, and so are all the combinations of the other six chakras. The full reading is paid for once, with no subscription, and includes all 20 sections — from money and relationships to the reading by decades.

sections.h2: What this guide is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, Vishuddha’s physics J = A + E, energy K = B + E, emotions their sum; every number over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The list of combinations and the most common and rarest variants were counted by going through every day from 1900 to 2099; the shares of arcana in the columns, through the dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card imagery** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922): Strength, the Hermit, Temperance, Judgement, the old titles of the Tower, the lists of meanings for the Magician, the High Priestess and the Hierophant. Quotations are given in Waite’s own words.
**The fifth position of the chakra spread** — Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 14, “The Seven Chakras Spread”.
**Tradition** — Purnananda, Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577), verses 28–31, in the translation by Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe), The Serpent Power (1919).

**Readings of the triples** — Arcana Sense’s own synthesis. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix, and neither describes physics / energy / emotions triples. Reading the row as one scene, the talent line in the energy of the upper chakras as “the gift coming down to the throat”, and every “Where it goes wrong” are our interpretation.

The destiny matrix is an esoteric model for self-observation with no scientific evidence behind it. The strengths and difficulties described here can be compared with your own experience; they do not describe the body and do not determine whether chakras are “open”.

faq.q: How do you read Vishuddha in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Work out the three numbers — physics is the day plus the centre, energy is the month plus the centre, emotions are their sum — or take them from the calculator. Read each one in its own column of the reference: the first is how you speak, the second what for, the third what you feel in response. Then put them together into one scene: what kind of conversation is typical for you and where it usually breaks down. The ready-made interpretation of your whole combination is in the full reading.

faq.q: What does it mean if physics and energy have the same number?
faq.a: This happens for about one date in sixteen. Most often it is when the day arcanum equals the number of the month: 5 May, 12 December, 23 May (23 → 5), 30 March (30 → 3). A repeat does not double the quality. One arcanum answers two different questions: how you speak and what for. Strength in both columns is a calm voice that never shouts and also the wish not to drop your thought under pressure.

faq.q: Why are the Magician and the High Priestess never found in Vishuddha?
faq.a: Because of the arithmetic. All three Vishuddha numbers include the centre of the chart, and the centre is itself a sum of four numbers and is never below 3. So neither physics, nor energy, nor emotions can drop below the Empress. There is an irony in this: among the Magician’s meanings Waite lists “skill, diplomacy”, and among the High Priestess’s, “silence”. The master of the word and the keeper of silence never turn up in the chakra of speech. It is a play of numbers, not a law, but it sticks in the mind.

faq.q: Which Vishuddha is the most common, and which is the rarest?
faq.a: People born from 1900 to 2099 get 379 different combinations. By variety this is the second row of the table after Anahata; Manipura, for comparison, has only 16 combinations. The most common is 11 / 14 / 7, yet even it goes to just one date in 182. The rarest is 5 / 3 / 8: in two hundred years exactly one day gets it, 1 August 2000.

faq.q: Is Vishuddha connected with the throat and the voice?
faq.a: Only as an image. The throat in the name “throat chakra” is its traditional place, not information about the body. The numbers of the matrix say nothing about timbre, volume or how you sing. They describe your manner of conversation, its motive and your response — things you can recognise in your own words.

faq.q: Is Vishuddha different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender does not affect the calculation: with the same date of birth the numbers are the same, and so is the interpretation. If an article gives a “female Vishuddha” tasks of its own, those are the author’s views, not the formula of the matrix.

faq.q: Can you “open” or “level up” your Vishuddha?
faq.a: The numbers do not change — they are calculated from the date of birth. What changes is how you handle your arcana. Each has a side where it helps and a side where it gets in the way: “Where it goes wrong” in the reference is about the second. In this sense, working with Vishuddha is very practical: notice your typical slip and next time do one step differently — hear the person out, name your interest out loud, don’t explain for the third time.

items.title: Anahata
level: Anahata is the level of love and relationships, and it is measured not by the number of romances but by the ability to stay close without losing yourself. A strong column here shows in one simple sign: other people are not afraid around such a person.

The skew goes two ways. A closed Anahata keeps its distance and explains it away as being busy; one thrown wide open gives everything and demands the same back, sending a bill for every act of care. The working state sits between these extremes: open, but with boundaries.

Closer to the centre than any other level: the left number of this row stands between the inner left point and the centre, the right one between the inner point of talent and the centre. That is why the level reads as the most personal — it is nearer to who someone is alone with themselves than to how others see them.

The third number of the row is not taken from the chart on its own — it is the sum of the first two, reduced. It shows no new theme, only what those two add up to when a person is in their feelings. Reading the row by one number is therefore pointless: a triple like “9 7 16” tells a single story, in which the third follows from the first two instead of arguing with them.

columns.text: The core: how attachment is felt and what someone does with jealousy, hurt and tenderness. In the minus it is either icy politeness or life on an emotional swing.

article.short: Anahata is the heart chakra, the fourth of seven. In the destiny matrix it is the fourth row of the chakra table, and its theme is closeness and mutual care: how you love, what keeps you beside a person and what you feel while you are there. The row holds three arcana. Physics shows what your love looks like in action. Energy shows what feeds your care and what makes it fade. Emotions show how closeness resonates inside you. The first two numbers come from the two points that stand nearest the centre of the chart; the third is their sum. Anahata takes arcana from 3 to 22: The Magician and The High Priestess never land here. There are 393 possible rows, and even the most common, 5 / 5 / 10, comes up on roughly one date in 145.

intro: Below: how to work out your row by hand, how to check the calculation against your year of birth in ten seconds, what each arcanum means in each column, and how three cards add up to one picture.

sections.h2: Anahata in the matrix: a heart right beside the centre of the chart
paragraphs: **Where it sits.** Take the two rays that run into the centre of the matrix: the left one starts from the arcanum of your birth day, the top one from your birth month. Each ray carries several points, and the last one before the centre belongs to Anahata: on the left ray it is point S (physics), on the top ray point T (energy). Nowhere on the chart is there a point closer to the centre. Anahata stands right up against the core of the matrix.

**What it is made of.** Point S is the sum of the inner left point and the centre; point T is the sum of the inner point of talent, the inner point at the top, and the centre. The inner points make up the Vishuddha row, and the centre is Manipura. So in the matrix Anahata is counted from its two neighbours: Manipura, the chakra of will, is added to Vishuddha, the chakra of the word. That is how the formula is built, not proof of anything, but the rhyme is exact: in this scheme, the way you love is put together from what you say and what you stand on.

**What it is about.** The Sanskrit word anahata is usually translated as “unstruck” or “unhurt”: in the yogic tradition it names the sound that rings by itself, without any blow. Anahata is the middle one of the seven chakras. The three below it are in charge of support, desire and will; the three above it, of the word, understanding and meaning. In the tarot tradition our readings draw on, the theme of the heart is wider than romance. Benebell Wen, the author of Holistic Tarot, writes that the heart chakra position in her spread “indicates love and relationships, though it might also speak more generally about the Seeker’s compassion for humanity, sense of charity and benevolence.” In essence, she says, this card shows **“how kind the Seeker is”**, and through that, how the person approaches love.

That is why Anahata in the matrix is not “the romance chakra”. It is your way of being close to anyone at all: a partner, your mother, a friend, a child, a colleague who is going through a bad patch. And it runs in two directions: the theme of the row is **mutual** care, that is, how you give warmth and how you take it in. Quite often one of the two comes easier than the other.

paragraphs.h3: Anahata, the relationship line and the “arcanum under the heart” are not the same thing

paragraphs: These three get mixed up all the time, although they are counted from different points and answer different questions.

head: Anahata
Relationship line M–R1–R
“Under the heart” (point R1)
rows: the fourth row of the chakra table
a line in the lower right part of the chart
the middle of the relationship line
how you love in general: care, need, feeling
the couple’s script: the way in, the main knot, everyday life and money
what becomes the couple’s main question once the first attraction has passed

paragraphs: If you came here looking for the “arcanum under the heart”, you need point R1, which has an article of its own. Anahata explains something else: why you care the way you do, with everyone and not only within a couple.

sections.h2: How to work out your Anahata from your date of birth in a minute
paragraphs: All you need is addition and one rule: **if a sum is greater than 22, add its digits** (23 → 5, 29 → 11, 40 → 4). Repeat until you get a number from 1 to 22.

ol: **A** is the day of birth: 4 → 4, 25 → 7, 31 → 4.
**B** is the number of the month.
**C** is the sum of the digits of the year: 1993 → 22, 1985 → 23 → 5.
**D** = A + B + C. **E** (the centre) = A + B + C + D.
Inner points: **J** = A + E, **K** = B + E. This is the Vishuddha row.
**Anahata’s physics** S = J + E. **Energy** T = K + E. **Emotions** = S + T.

paragraphs: Example: someone born on 4 March 1993.

The Anahata row is **12 / 11 / 5**. If you already have your chakra table, there is no need to start from scratch: add the centre (the Manipura number) to Vishuddha’s physics and energy. 8 + 4 = 12, 7 + 4 = 11, and you get the same row.
If you would rather not count by hand, the calculator builds the whole chakra table at once. The arcana are shown free of charge and with no sign-up.

paragraphs.h3: The birth-year check: the third number knows your year

paragraphs: Anahata has a property that almost nobody writes about. **Add up the digits of your year of birth, then add the third number of your Anahata: the result is a multiple of nine, that is 9, 18, 27, 36 or 45.**

ul: 15 July 1985: 1 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 23; Anahata for this date is 15 / 7 / 22, and 23 + 22 = **45**.

paragraphs: Why it works. Write the Anahata formula out in full and you will find that the day and the month each enter the emotions exactly nine times. Adding digits does not change the remainder after division by nine, so as the sums are reduced, the day and the month drop out and only the year is left. We tested the rule on all 46,021 dates from 1900 to 2025, and there are no exceptions.

Two practical conclusions follow. First, if the check does not add up, the calculation has a mistake in it, most often a missed reduction of a number above 22. Second, everyone born in the same year has one of just two or three possible third numbers in Anahata.

head: Year of birth
Anahata emotions
rows: 4 · The Emperor, 13 · Death or 22 · The Fool
3 · The Empress, 12 · The Hanged Man or 21 · The World
10 · The Wheel of Fortune or 19 · The Sun

paragraphs: The rows repeat every nine years: 1944 belongs with 1953, and 2026 with 2017. Where there are two options, the smaller number comes up in roughly three cases out of four. Which one you get is decided by your day and month. This is a property of the formula, not a “generational feeling”: the year narrows the choice to two or three cards, and the date does the rest.

paragraphs.h3: Anahata 9 / 7 / 16: what it means and how to check the sum

paragraphs: If your Anahata shows 9, 7 and 1, go back over the calculation. In the classic matrix The Magician (1) never lands in Anahata, in any column, and the third number is always the sum of the first two. 9 + 7 = 16, so the correct row is **9 / 7 / 16**: The Hermit in physics, The Chariot in energy, The Tower in emotions. The year check confirms it. This Anahata only occurs for people born in 1982, 1991, 2000, 2009 and 2018, and in the earlier years of the same series: 1973, 1964, 1955. Take 3 January 1982: 1 + 9 + 8 + 2 = 20, and 20 + 16 = 36.

How it reads. The Hermit in action: you first think things through on your own and come to the person you love with words already weighed. The Chariot in motive: you care where the relationship is heading, and you need a shared road and a next step. The Tower in feeling: if that road rested on things left unsaid, the discovery feels not like a crack but like a collapse. The strength of this row is forethought: it is easy to lean on someone who arrives not on impulse but with a plan. The weak spot is in the same place: a plan made alone is easily mistaken for a shared one. So the main check for 9 / 7 / 16 is to ask the other person what they think before the route is ready, not after.

sections.h2: How to read Anahata: three numbers, one picture
paragraphs: The reference below gives the meaning of every card in every column. But a row is not three separate labels. It is easier to read in four steps.

ol: **Write out the row with the column names.** The order matters: 12 / 11 / 5 and 11 / 12 / 5 are different rows, and both occur.
**Read each card in its own column:** physics is the action, energy the motive, emotions the feeling.
**Find one sentence that ties all three together.** Not “The Hanged Man plus Strength plus The Hierophant”, but a thought you can recognise in your own life.
**Look for the difficulty along the same lines.** A row’s weak spot is usually its strength pushed to the limit.

paragraphs: Here is how it works in practice. Below is Anahata 12 / 11 / 5 from the full reading, word for word.

**Riding out their storm, keeping the bond** 12 · The Hanged Man — pausing to see their side. 11 · Strength — holding strong feelings steady. 5 · The Hierophant — trust in shared promises. With you, someone close doesn’t have to keep up a brave face. Care in Anahata begins with The Hanged Man: you set your own affairs aside and look at what is happening through the other person’s eyes, in no hurry to hand over ready-made advice. Strength fuels this involvement: you want to stay close when feelings run high, without suppressing either the feelings or the person. Trust comes through The Hierophant — in a relationship that has a recognised shape: promises, traditions, your own “this is how we do things”. After a hard day, someone close to you snaps and says more than they mean. You don’t answer in kind, and you don’t rush to fix their mood. You listen until the storm dies down, even though you had other plans for the evening — and behind the sharpness you make out the exhaustion. The next morning, the usual breakfast together says without words: we’re still us. **Around you, strong feelings don’t break the bond — they have somewhere to settle.** One person easily drops out of this picture — you. Seeing through the other’s eyes comes so naturally that your own things keep being put off: plans can wait, hurt can wait, a request can wait too. You calm your own storms as carefully as anyone else’s — and the person close to you may not even know you’re struggling. What’s left is holding on to the form: “this is what people do in a good relationship”. But when it replaces a real conversation, care becomes a duty done by the rulebook: everything is done properly, yet there is less and less warmth.

Look at what has been done here. Strength is read not as force or self-assurance but as the ability to ride out someone else’s storm: not answering in kind, not rushing to fix their mood, but hearing them out. The Hanged Man is not patience but a readiness to drop your plans for the evening and see the exhaustion behind the sharpness. The Hierophant holds the bond together through form: the usual breakfast the next morning says without words that you are still you. The trap grew out of the same combination: in this kind of care it is easy to forget yourself, and the form starts to stand in for a real conversation. Change one card and the picture changes. Every one of the 393 rows in the reading is written this way.

sections.h2: The arcana in Anahata: what each number means in all three columns
paragraphs: Anahata takes 20 arcana, from The Empress (3) to The Fool (22). The most frequent card here is The Hierophant: it appears in the row in 22% of calculations. The rarest is The Hanged Man, at 9%. First a cheat sheet to help you find your cards quickly, then each card in detail.

head: Arcanum
Physics: how you love in practice
Energy: what keeps you close
Emotions: what you feel
rows: taking charge of how life is run
keeping your word and your customs
the joy of choosing each other
the lift of a shared stride
a firm word in a gentle voice
not acting in the heat of the moment
a feeling that needs a pause
letting go of the old image
the sadness and relief of change
a strong pull towards your person
helping a dream along with deeds
believing in the person you love
a fine response and anxious guesses
being openly glad of the person
the call of your own people, belonging
a whole where each stays themselves
trying things together for the first time

paragraphs: For each card below you will find its image in the theme of the heart, the three columns and the trap: what this strength turns into if it goes unnoticed. These are symbolic themes to recognise yourself in, not verdicts on your character.
In Waite, The Empress is “the fruitful mother of thousands”, “all that is symbolized by the visible house of man”. In Anahata this is care that makes everything around it grow and feel lived in.

ul: **Physics:** care you can touch: feeding, warming, making things cosy, bringing a blanket at the right moment. Your love shows in your home.
**Energy:** the wish to make things grow, to see the person you love flourish and what you share grow stronger: a home, a family, a joint venture.
**Emotions:** the warmth of plenty. Joy when care comes back to you and “we have everything we need”.
**Trap:** care nobody asked for. Feeding someone who isn’t hungry and taking offence when they leave food on the plate. One day “I do so much for you” gets said out loud, and care turns into a debt.

paragraphs.h3: 4 · The Emperor: love as a solid roof

paragraphs: Waite writes that this card and that of the Empress “do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied”. His Emperor is “executive and realization, the power of this world”. In Anahata this is love expressed through running things and keeping them safe.

ul: **Physics:** taking on the running of your shared life: plans, money, repairs, safety. Your “I love you” sounds like “I’ll take care of it” and is proved by what gets done.
**Energy:** a need for stability and clear boundaries. You want to stay where the ground is firm underfoot and it is clear who is responsible for what.
**Emotions:** calm that comes from predictability. Irritation when the order is changed without you.

**Trap:** safety quietly turns into control: where are you, how much did you spend, why isn’t this going to plan. Wen pictures the price of such rule as a parched kingdom: there is order, but less and less life in it.

paragraphs.h3: 5 · The Hierophant: love that rests on what you share

paragraphs: The most common card in Anahata. In Waite’s list of divinatory meanings The Hierophant stands for “marriage, alliance” and, “by another account, mercy and goodness”. This is love that rests on shared values, customs and a word that is never broken.

ul: **Physics:** taking the union seriously. Keeping your word and cherishing customs: anniversaries, Sunday phone calls, the family table.
**Energy:** leaning on shared values. You stay when it is clear what you both believe in and what you are together for.
**Emotions:** trust in a shared word. Disappointment when the other person lives by different rules of “a proper relationship”.

**Trap:** form instead of meaning. Waite warns that the pontiff may forget “the significance of this his symbolic state” and act “as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies”. In a relationship these are rituals still kept after real conversation has stopped, or a “this is how it’s done in our family” that matters more than a living person.

paragraphs.h3: 6 · The Lovers: love as a mutual choice

paragraphs: Waite calls this “in all simplicity the card of human love”: two people stand unveiled before each other, in a love not yet “contaminated by gross material desire”. Wen adds the theme of choice. In Anahata this is love in which two people choose each other openly and freely. The Lovers turn up in roughly one calculated row in five.

ul: **Physics:** choosing the person plainly: saying “I’m with you”, introducing them to your friends, answering honestly, not leaving the relationship hanging.
**Energy:** a drive towards mutuality. It matters that both of you choose, by consent and not out of duty or fear of being alone.
**Emotions:** the joy of choosing each other, the tenderness of two people with nothing to hide from each other.

**Trap:** checking every decision of your own against the other person’s reaction, or demanding that the choice be confirmed anew every day. Mutuality turns into an exam that can never be passed for good.

paragraphs.h3: 7 · The Chariot: love on the move

paragraphs: Waite’s Chariot is “above all things triumph in the mind”, a conquest on planes that are “manifest or external and not within himself”. In Anahata this is love that needs a shared road and visible progress.

ul: **Physics:** taking the initiative. Suggesting a move, dreaming up a trip, steering a shared plan.
**Energy:** the wish to move forward together. A relationship is alive as long as you can see where you are going and there is a next step.
**Emotions:** excitement and the lift of a shared stride, the joy of a shared win.

**Trap:** driving for two. Waite’s charioteer wins on the outside, and in a couple you can likewise win the argument and lose the closeness, or rush the relationship forward without asking whether the other person wants to go there, and at that pace.

paragraphs: For Waite, Justice is the moral principle “which deals unto every man according to his works”. But beside it he sets gifts of another order, which “we have them or have not”, and adds that “the law of Justice is not however involved by either alternative”. In Anahata this is love that needs clarity and equal respect. In the emotions column Justice is one of the two most common cards.

ul: **Physics:** honestly carrying your share: agreeing who does what, and doing what was agreed.
**Energy:** a need for mutual respect: taking both people into account, deciding so that it is fair to both.
**Emotions:** relief once everything has been said. Hurt when an expectation nobody voiced is broken.

**Trap:** bookkeeping in love: “that’s the second time I’ve given in”, “I put in more”. Agreements live by the law of Justice, but love, as we read it, is closer to the gifts in that same passage of Waite: it is not credited according to merit.

paragraphs: Waite’s Hermit stands on a height holding up a lamp that is not wrapped in his mantle: “where I am, you also may be.” In Anahata this is love that speaks quietly and thinks before it takes a step. In the emotions column it is the most common card, level with Justice.

ul: **Physics:** being quietly there: listening, giving room, not crowding. Thinking it over alone before suggesting anything.
**Energy:** a need to make sense of the relationship on your own: time and space to understand what you feel.
**Emotions:** a deep, restrained feeling that does not show at once. It is there; it simply lives deep down.

**Trap:** the lamp under the cloak. You went off to think, and the person you love decided they had been rejected. The love is there, but the other cannot see it. One sentence uncovers the lamp: “I need a little quiet. It’s not about you.”

paragraphs.h3: 10 · The Wheel of Fortune: love in waves

paragraphs: Waite sees in the Wheel “the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe” and “the flux of human life”, and stresses its “essential idea of stability amidst movement”. In Anahata these are relationships that live through stages and turns.

ul: **Physics:** flexibly rearranging your shared life when life turns a corner: a move, a new job, the birth of a child.
**Energy:** an interest in new stages. The relationship holds as long as it keeps renewing itself.
**Emotions:** feelings in waves: a lift at the turns, a lull on the straight stretches.

**Trap:** mistaking a lull for the end. Or waiting for the right moment to raise a question that has been piling up, and the moment never comes. The axle the changes turn on is one you have to hold yourselves.

paragraphs.h3: 11 · Strength: strong feeling in gentle hands

paragraphs: On Waite’s card a woman closes the jaws of a lion that “is being led by a chain of flowers”. The chain of flowers, he explains, signifies, among many other things, “the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”, and the card “has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense”. In Anahata this is the ability to stay in touch when things run hot.

ul: **Physics:** a firm word in a gentle voice. Saying something unpleasant with care, hearing disagreement out without steamrolling it.
**Energy:** staying close under strain, neither running from a quarrel nor going on the attack.
**Emotions:** strong attachment and compassion that need no damping down. The feeling is big, and the hands are gentle.

**Trap:** being strong for two for too long. Bottling up, smoothing over, “keeping it together”, until the lion breaks the chain of flowers. And separately: the gentleness of Strength does not oblige you to put up with what is destroying you.

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man: seeing it from the other side

paragraphs: The rarest card in Anahata. Waite insists that the Hanged Man’s face expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”: this is “life in suspension, but life and not death”. Readings of the card as martyrdom and duty he calls false. In Anahata this is the pause in which you have time to see the situation through the other person’s eyes.

ul: **Physics:** not acting in the heat of the moment. Stopping, holding back your own rush, letting the person reach the decision themselves.
**Energy:** the wish to understand how it all looks from their side, and to see beyond your own desire.
**Emotions:** a feeling that needs a pause. You feel deeply but not at once, sometimes together with the other person’s pain.
**Trap:** the pause turns into sacrifice. Waiting, enduring, putting yourself off “for the sake of peace” is no longer Waite’s Hanged Man but the very martyrdom he argued against.

paragraphs: On Waite’s card the horseman “carries no visible weapon”, and his black banner bears the Mystic Rose, “which signifies life”. The card itself, for him, is “change, transformation and passage”. In Anahata this is the ability to end what has served its time in a relationship: habits, roles, rules. Not necessarily the relationship itself.

ul: **Physics:** closing what has outlived itself through action: changing routines, scrapping old rules, ending the habits of “the people you used to be”.
**Energy:** a readiness to let go of the old image of the person you love and meet the one they have become.
**Emotions:** sadness and relief together. The end of a stage is lived deeply: the children have grown up, the roles have changed, the past cannot be brought back.
**Trap:** clinging to a dead form out of fear of change, or, the other way round, cutting everything off when a single habit has run its course. The card does not predict break-ups.

paragraphs: Waite’s angel pours “the essences of life from chalice to chalice”, with one foot on the earth and one on the waters. The card, in Waite’s words, “tempers, combines and harmonises”. In her example about relationships, Wen ties it to “a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions”. In Anahata this is closeness built in small steps and at a shared pace.

ul: **Physics:** drawing closer in small, steady steps, matching different paces, agreeing on little things.
**Energy:** joining two lives without cancelling either, finding a shared measure.
**Emotions:** an even warmth that does not cool even in an argument.

**Trap:** peace at any price. Muting what is unpleasant for the sake of seeming agreement, and accepting a compromise that erases a boundary that matters to you. Coming to terms does not require giving yourself up.

paragraphs.h3: 15 · The Devil: the pull that holds

paragraphs: In Waite, two figures are chained to the Devil “as if Adam and Eve after the Fall”: this is “the chain and fatality of the material life”. He also notes that the one exalted above them is not “to be their master for ever”. And the Devil’s raised hand is, in Waite, “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant”, the most common card in Anahata. In Anahata The Devil is a strong pull and attachment. It appears in the row in 12% of calculations.

ul: **Physics:** closeness you can touch: gifts, shared things and money, physical closeness. You bind your lives together firmly.
**Energy:** a strong pull towards your person, an attraction that holds.
**Emotions:** clinging attachment, passion side by side with the fear of loss.

**Trap:** losing the difference between “I want to be with you” and “I want you to be mine”. Jealousy, checking up, “I can’t live without you”. The number itself says nothing about dependence: it shows how strongly you attach, and what you do with that force is up to you.

paragraphs: Waite reads the Tower as the rending of “a House of Falsehood” and recalls the psalm: “except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.” In Anahata this is love that cannot stand falseness. The Tower appears in the row in 12% of calculations.

ul: **Physics:** naming plainly what doesn’t work. Talking about hard things out loud and revising rules that have outlived themselves.
**Energy:** a need for an honest foundation. Where something rests on an untruth, you feel uneasy.
**Emotions:** a sharp response to untruth. A lie that comes out feels not like a crack but like a collapse.
**Trap:** bringing everything down in the moment of the blow. The Tower destroys a house of lies, not every house. Before you decide for good, separate the checked fact from the guess.

paragraphs.h3: 17 · The Star: faith in the other

paragraphs: Waite gives the Star’s mottoes as “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. Her figure pours water on both land and sea, and her gift, in Waite, reaches those below “in the measure that they can receive her influx”. In Anahata this is generous tenderness and faith in the person you love.

ul: **Physics:** helping a dream along with deeds: finding a course, freeing up an evening, being the first to look at the work.
**Energy:** the inspiration of growing side by side. It matters to you to believe in the person and to watch them grow bigger.
**Emotions:** generous tenderness and hope.

**Trap:** loving an image instead of a person, so that the one you love has to live up to your dream of them. Or giving more than the other can take in. In Waite the measure is the capacity to receive, not the generosity of the giver.

paragraphs: Waite’s Moon is a path walked when “there is only reflected light to guide it”, where the dog and the wolf are “the fears of the natural mind”. In Anahata this is a fine sense of atmosphere and subtext.

ul: **Physics:** gentleness with what is unclear. You notice that something is off and approach it softly.
**Energy:** sensitivity to mood, hearing what lies beneath the words.
**Emotions:** a fine response to the other person’s state, and anxious guesses when you are near them.

**Trap:** filling in the dark. A short reply turns into “they’ve gone cold”, and you are now reacting to your own version. The Moon’s observation is often right; it is the explanation that goes wrong. The check is simple: ask.

paragraphs: Waite’s Sun is direct light, “the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light”, and that light is “typified by the heart of a child”. In Anahata this is love that is not hidden.

ul: **Physics:** being openly glad of the person: hugging them in front of everyone, praising them, celebrating together.
**Energy:** sharing warmth and living without things left unsaid.
**Emotions:** the joy of being accepted as you are.
**Trap:** shining in the hope of a reflection. If there was less attention than you hoped for, you dim or start chasing admiration. The Sun shines; it does not wait to be shone on.

paragraphs: Waite’s Judgement is transformation in answer to a summons that “is heard and answered from within”. On the card a man, a woman and their child rise from their tombs, but Waite deliberately adds others: “there are more than three who are restored”, and a reading through the family alone falls short. In Anahata this is the renewal of familiar roles and a sense of belonging.

ul: **Physics:** changing what you inherited through action. Seeing family roles from the outside and rebuilding them: who decides, who does the caring, how you quarrel.
**Energy:** answering the call of your own people, a need to belong and for a living bond.
**Emotions:** moments of clarity, when you can see that a stage is over and the relationship has come back to life.
**Trap:** repeating your parents’ script without noticing, or waiting for years for the person you love to “wake up” and change on their own.

paragraphs.h3: 21 · The World: a whole where each stays themselves

paragraphs: For Waite the World is fullness and completion, “the rapture of the universe when it understands itself in God”. In Anahata this is love with enough room for two different worlds.

ul: **Physics:** living broadly as two: joining your shared life with friends, work and separate interests.
**Energy:** seeing the union as a whole and accepting differences.
**Emotions:** a sense of a whole in which each of you stays yourself.
**Trap:** the picture of a harmonious couple becomes more important than an awkward conversation. A particular difficulty gets talked around with general words about how good everything is overall.

paragraphs.h3: 22 · The Fool: lightness and room to breathe

paragraphs: In the matrix 22 is The Fool; in Waite his number is 0. He is “the spirit in search of experience”, and for him “the edge which opens on the depth has no terror”. In Anahata this is love that needs air, play and novelty.

ul: **Physics:** trying things together for the first time: surprising each other, fooling around, turning off the familiar route.
**Energy:** room and lively interest. You want to be close as long as the relationship has air in it.
**Emotions:** carefree, almost childlike joy.
**Trap:** any commitment feels like a cage. Instead of the words “I need space”, a sudden disappearance. And the beginning delights more than what follows.

paragraphs: The reference answers the question “what does my card mean”. The question “what do my three cards mean together” is answered by the reading of the row, which is covered below.

sections.h2: Doubles, mirrors and rarities: Anahata by the numbers
paragraphs: We calculated Anahata for every date from 1 January 1900 to 31 December 2025, 46,021 dates in all. Here is what they show.

**One card in two columns.** Physics and energy match in 6.7% of calculations: 5 / 5 / 10, 9 / 9 / 18, 17 / 17 / 7 and so on, and a double is possible for each of the 20 arcana. A repeat does not mean “double strength”. One card shows itself in two roles, in action and in motive. In the row 5 / 5 / 10, The Hierophant in physics is loyalty to customs, and in energy it is reliance on shared views. A match is only possible when the day and the month of birth leave the same remainder after division by nine, as for people born on 3, 12, 21 or 30 March. But even for them it does not always happen.

**The Moon as a mirror.** When The Moon stands in physics or energy (this happens in 11% of calculations), in four cases out of ten the emotions repeat the other card: 18 / 6 / 6, 7 / 18 / 7, 18 / 9 / 9. The reason is arithmetic: add 18 to a number from 5 to 11, reduce the sum, and you get the same number back. But the rhyme with the card is exact. Waite’s Moon is reflected light, and in these rows the feeling reflects the neighbouring card. Read such a row this way: the feeling grows out of the other card, and The Moon adds a half-tone to it, a sensitivity and a habit of filling in the gaps.

**The most common and the rarest.** The most common Anahata is 5 / 5 / 10: 318 dates out of 46,021, roughly one date in 145. The rarest are 4 / 12 / 16 and 12 / 4 / 16. Each turned up only twice in 126 years, and all four dates fall in 2000: 4 and 31 March, 3 and 30 April.

**The “scary” cards.** Death, The Devil or The Tower stand in almost every third calculated Anahata, 31.6% of dates. Add The Moon and the figure reaches 43%. This is no verdict on your relationships: in the theme of the heart, each of these cards has a working side, whether honesty, the ability to end what has outlived itself, the strength of attachment or sensitivity.

**Which numbers never appear.** The Magician (1) and The High Priestess (2) never land in Anahata: both of its points come from addition, the small sums here are always greater than two, and the large ones reduce to between 3 and 12. In the emotions column small numbers come up more often: 11 or lower in 69% of calculations, while each number from 13 to 21 accounts for only 2–3%.
**The order of the columns matters.** 12 / 11 / 5 and 11 / 12 / 5 are different rows: in the first The Hanged Man stands in action, in the second in motive.

sections.h2: A “closed” Anahata, Anahata “in the minus” and other myths
paragraphs: **“My Anahata is closed, empty, weak.”** The row cannot tell you that. The numbers in the table are card numbers, not scores for how full something is: 22 is not “stronger” than 3, and The Sun is not “better” than The Tower. In the classic calculation all seven rows are always filled; there is no such thing as an empty chakra.

**“Anahata in the minus.”** “Plus” and “minus” are best understood as two ways of living the same row, not as a property of the person. The Hermit in emotions in the plus is a deep, quiet feeling. In the minus it is a feeling the person you love knows nothing about. The card is the same; the difference is whether the other person can see it.

**“Bad numbers.”** Death in Anahata does not predict a break-up, The Devil does not predict betrayal, and The Tower does not predict disaster. Each number describes how you love, not what will happen to you.

**“Anahata is the heart as an organ.”** No. The matrix says nothing about the body, and no number in this row describes how you feel physically. If something is troubling you physically, that is a question for a specialist, not for the matrix.
**“Anahata has to be opened or worked through.”** The numbers do not change. What changes is how you live your row. Three questions are enough to begin with, one for each column:

ul: **physics:** does my care give the person I love what they need, or what I know how to give?
**energy:** do I say out loud what I need in order to stay close?
**emotions:** does the person I love know what I feel, or do I just assume it is obvious anyway?

faq.q: Which arcana are bad in Anahata?
faq.a: None. At least one of these cards appears in 43% of Anahata calculations for dates from 1900 to 2025.

faq.q: Why does another calculator give me different numbers?

faq.q: Are Anahata and the “arcanum under the heart” the same thing?
faq.a: No. “Under the heart” is the name for the partner point R1, the middle of the relationship line. Anahata is the chakra row about how you love and care for everyone close to you, not only within a couple.

faq.q: Is Anahata different for men and women?

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice and 11 Strength?
