article.title: The Manipura chakra in the destiny matrix: fire at the very centre of the chart
article.short: Manipura is the third chakra, the chakra of fire. In the destiny matrix its theme is will and independence. Its three numbers answer three questions: how you take on a task, what keeps you going, and how you live through the outcome — success, rejection, other people’s judgement. All three numbers come from a single point, the centre of the matrix. That is why the first two numbers in the row are always the same and the third is their sum: 4 / 4 / 8, 7 / 7 / 14, 10 / 10 / 20. There are only 16 such rows, and every one of them is covered below. To find yours, add up three numbers from your date of birth and look the sum up in the table.

sections.h2: What Manipura is: the city of jewels and the chakra of fire
paragraphs: The name is Sanskrit: mani means jewel, pura means city. In the Indian tradition it is the third of the seven chakras, counting from the bottom, and its element is fire. The fullest description comes from Purnananda’s treatise Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577), which Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe) translated into English in The Serpent Power (1919). According to the treatise, Manipura lies at the root of the navel. It is a lotus of ten petals, the colour of heavy rain clouds. Inside it is a triangular region of fire that shines like the rising sun. There Vahni, the god of fire, sits on a ram, and his seed syllable is “Ram”. The solar plexus and the colour yellow came later, from modern Western charts that paint the seven chakras in the colours of the rainbow.

In her textbook Holistic Tarot, Benebell Wen gives this chakra a position in the Seven Chakras Spread. She reads the card in that position for career issues, level of achievement and persistence. The chakra, she writes, **“relates to the ego, personal power, the wheel of force, and how much drive the Seeker possesses for success in his or her career”**. The Sanskrit word chakra itself means “wheel”.
In the destiny matrix Manipura covers more than a career: its theme is **will and independence**. Manipura answers these questions:

ul: which tasks you take on gladly and which only by forcing yourself;
how you act when the decision is yours;
what keeps you from giving up: growth, order, the thrill, the truth, freedom;
what happens inside you when the result arrives: praise, rejection, failure, uncertainty;
where independence turns into control, haste or dodging the conversation.

paragraphs: What Manipura does not show: the size of your income, your job title or the state of your digestion. Its numbers describe how you act, not how much you have already achieved.

sections.h2: Where Manipura sits in the destiny matrix: right in the centre
paragraphs: The destiny matrix is an eight-pointed star made of two squares. The personal square has four points: the day arcanum (A) on the left, the month (B) at the top, the year (C) on the right and their sum (D) at the bottom. In the middle of the star stands point E, the sum of all four. On the site it is labelled the centre of the chart: the baseline state a person returns to after any strain.

Every other chakra takes two different points. Sahasrara takes the day and the month, Muladhara the year and the bottom point, and the rest take inner points between the edge of the star and the centre. Manipura takes one point twice: both physics and energy are the centre. That is why its row always looks like “X / X / X + X”.

Yet the centre does not stay in its own row. All the inner points are counted from it: J = A + E, K = B + E, L = C + E, M = D + E. This is how the Manipura number finds its way into the calculation of four more chakras. Here is what that looks like for 24.03.1985, where the centre is 10:

paragraphs: Anahata even takes the centre twice: first through Vishuddha, then once more directly.

The anatomical solar plexus is a knot of nerves from which branches run out to the organs of the abdomen. Manipura in the matrix works in a similar way: from the centre, numbers run out into five rows of the table. It is only an image, but an easy one to remember.

None of this makes Manipura more important than the other chakras: each row is read on its own. But it does lead to something worth knowing. If you and a friend share the same Manipura, your other six rows are almost certainly different. The centre is shared, but the day, the month and the year belong to each of you alone.

sections.h2: Why the first two numbers match — and why that is not a mistake
paragraphs: Someone sees 7 / 7 / 14 in the row and decides either that the calculator is broken or that they have a “double Chariot”, and so twice the drive. Neither is true. Here one arcanum answers two different questions.

ul: **Physics — how you act.** How you take on a task, plan, negotiate and carry the work through to a result.
**Energy — what gives you strength.** Why you get involved at all, and what helps you not to give up halfway.
**Emotions — how you live through the result.** Success, rejection, judgement, uncertainty. This number is the sum of the first two, but it is read as a separate question.

paragraphs: Take 7 / 7 / 14. In physics The Chariot means driving the work towards a finishing line: choosing a direction and keeping different forces in one harness. In energy the same Chariot becomes fuel: strength comes from the movement itself, from each stretch of road left behind. In the first case it is the reins; in the second, the joy of the road. Temperance in emotions adds a sense of measure: success does not go to your head, and a rejection does not sting for long.

In other chakras physics and energy are set by two different arcana, and there can be tension between them: you do one thing, but your strength comes from another. In Manipura one arcanum answers both questions, so method and motive speak the same language. The most surprising thing in this row is the third number. It shows what happens to you when the work meets its result.
And that third number cannot be read from a dictionary. Justice stands in emotions in three different Manipuras, and in the full reading each has its own caption:

paragraphs: The card shows a woman with a sword and scales, and Waite sees in her **“the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works”**. It is one card, but it weighs different things: next to The Emperor, the assessment of your contribution; next to Death, the debts left over when something ends; next to The Fool, the price of a bold leap. The pairs 3 / 3 / 6 and 12 / 12 / 6, with The Lovers in emotions, work the same way, and so do 5 / 5 / 10 and 14 / 14 / 10, with The Wheel of Fortune.

sections.h2: Which numbers Manipura can hold, and which it never does
paragraphs: There are only 16 rows, and they turn up at very different rates. Below is the share of each among all dates of birth since 1900:
Manipura depends only on the sum A + B + C, so people born on different days, in different months and years can share a row. If yours is one of the common ones, roughly one date in nine has it too.

**Six arcana never appear in Manipura at all:** The Magician (1), The High Priestess (2), The Devil (15), The Star (17), The Sun (19) and The World (21). They do not turn up in any of the three columns for any date. The reason lies in how the centre is built. It is made of the sum A + B + C plus the same sum again, only reduced, so in effect the sum is doubled. Numbers from 14 upwards come almost only from small sums. Doubling them needs no reduction, so the result is even. The odd numbers 15, 17, 19 and 21 never land in the centre, and 1 and 2 cannot come out either directly or after reduction.

A curious coincidence: the treatise compares Manipura’s fire to the rising sun, popular charts place it at the solar plexus, and yet The Sun never lands in this chakra. There is no point looking for meaning in this: it is arithmetic, not symbolism.

**The rarest Manipura is 16 / 16 / 5.** Between 1900 and 1999 it went only to people born on 1 or 2 January or on 1 February, and not in every year: just 17 dates in the whole century. For dates in the 2000s the rare rows come up almost three times as often as across the 20th century as a whole: 4.2% of dates against about one and a half per cent. A year like 2000 or 2003 gives a small number, so the sum of the date comes out small too.

sections.h2: Manipura 10 / 10 / 20 in the destiny matrix: The Wheel of Fortune and Judgement
paragraphs: This is one of the most common rows: about 11% of dates of birth. It comes up when A + B + C equals 5, 14, 23, 32, 41 or 50 — for example, for people born on 24.03.1985, 17.11.1975 or 11.04.1997.

**Physics and energy: 10, The Wheel of Fortune.** Waite describes the wheel as the perpetual motion of the universe and the flux of human life. The Sphinx on it stands for equilibrium, or, in Waite’s words, **“stability amidst movement”**. Behind the symbol Waite sees **“the denial of chance”**, so this is not a card of blind luck. In physics the Wheel shows how you act: you notice that circumstances have turned, rework the plan and catch the moment. In energy it becomes fuel. Your strength grows once the work starts moving, and sameness, where nothing changes, drains it.

**Emotions: 20, Judgement.** An angel sounds the trumpet and people rise from their tombs. Waite reads the scene as a transformation in answer to a summons, **“which summons is heard and answered from within”**, and asks: **“What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response?”** This is how the result is felt in Manipura. Success or failure sounds like a signal that a stage is complete and it is time to move on to the next. Judgement here is neither punishment nor a sentence. It is the moment when it becomes clear where to go next. Judgement in the emotions of Manipura appears in this row only.

The arcanum’s role changes everything. In the rows 5 / 5 / 10 and 14 / 14 / 10 the Wheel stands in emotions: the turn happens to you, and you live through it. In 10 / 10 / 20 the Wheel stands in physics and energy: the turn is what you act with and what fires you up.

But Manipura is one row out of seven. The same person born on 24.03.1985 has Anahata 8 / 5 / 13, Vishuddha 16 / 13 / 11 and Svadhisthana 15 / 6 / 21. In the full reading each of these rows is read separately, with a text of its own. None of them can be found from the sum of three numbers the way Manipura can.

sections.h2: Is Manipura the money chakra?
paragraphs: Popular descriptions call Manipura the chakra of money, status and power. Wen uses it to look at career, achievement and persistence. In the destiny matrix Manipura shows how you work and how you live through the result, not how much you earn. **It is the chakra of the work, not of the wallet.**

What ties it to money is the work itself. The row 8 / 8 / 16 is about how you negotiate shares and terms. The row 4 / 4 / 8 says that you need authority, not just tasks. The row 9 / 9 / 18 is about finished work that stays out of sight for a long time while it is unclear how it will be judged. All of this affects what you earn, even though it names no sums.

There is a direct arithmetical link too. The entry of the money line is point L = year + centre, and the entry of relationships is point M = bottom point + centre. These are the same two numbers that stand in Svadhisthana. For 24.03.1985: L = 5 + 10 = 15, M = 14 + 10 = 24 → 6. The Manipura number goes into the sum for both the money entry and the relationship entry. But money is read along its own line: the entry, the direction, the crossing of the channels. Manipura alone is not enough for that.

sections.h2: “Blocked”, “weak”, “in minus”: what Manipura cannot show

ul: **The numbers name arcana; they are not scores.** 22 is not stronger than 3, and a rare row does not mean a special destiny. There is no such thing as an empty Manipura: everyone has three cards in it.
**Matching numbers do not mean imbalance.** Physics and energy coincide because of how the calculation works, and that is true for everyone. It shows neither an excess of fire nor a block.

**“Plus” and “minus” are not two different arcana but two modes of one.** The part of each reading above about where things go off track grows out of the same strength that is described in physics and energy. Instead of asking “how do I unblock my Manipura?”, it is more useful to ask: where does my way of acting go too far?
**Manipura says nothing about your physical condition.** Neither the digestive organs nor the “solar plexus” in the medical sense can be read from the numbers.

paragraphs: Seven chakras, three arcana in each: physics, energy, emotions. Manipura is row 03, and its first two numbers are always the same. The numbers and cards appear as soon as you run the calculation. The interpretation of each row opens in the full reading; until you pay, the row shows a lock.

faq.q: How do I calculate Manipura in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Add up the day arcanum, the month and the year arcanum (numbers above 22 are reduced by adding up their digits) and find the sum in the table above. Or work out the centre of the matrix: E = A + B + C + D. Manipura is E / E / E + E. Example: 24.03.1985 → 6 + 3 + 5 = 14 → 10 / 10 / 20.

faq.q: What does Manipura 10 / 10 / 20 mean?
faq.a: The Wheel of Fortune in physics and energy: you act in rhythm with change, and your strength grows once things start moving. Judgement in emotions: the result feels like a signal that a stage is complete and it is time for the next. The weak spot is a lull, when you want to wait for a sign instead of taking ordinary steps. More in the section on 10 / 10 / 20 above.

faq.q: Why are the first two numbers in Manipura the same?
faq.a: Because both columns take the same point — the centre of the matrix, E. It is a feature of the calculation, not a mistake and not “double strength”. In physics the arcanum is read as a way of acting, in energy as a source of strength.

faq.q: Where is Manipura in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In the centre of the matrix, at point E. In our chakra table it is row 03: we start from Muladhara and come to Manipura through Svadhisthana.

faq.q: Is Manipura the money chakra?
faq.a: It is more the chakra of work. It shows how you take on a job, negotiate and live through the result, but not the size of your income. The centre goes into the sum for the entry of the money line (L = year + centre), but money itself is read along its own line.

faq.q: How can I tell if my Manipura is blocked or weak?
faq.a: Not from the numbers. Arcanum numbers are not scores, and there is no such thing as an empty Manipura. It is more useful to look at where your way of acting goes too far: every row above describes this in its part about where things go off track.

faq.q: Why do The Sun, The Devil and The World never appear in Manipura?
faq.a: The centre of the matrix is in effect a doubled sum of the date, so the large numbers in it are always even. 15, 17, 19 and 21 do not come up for any date of birth, and neither do 1 and 2. In all, 16 rows are possible in Manipura.

faq.q: Why does another calculator show different numbers?
faq.a: Most often it comes down to reduction. Here the digits are added up: 12 + 12 = 24 → 2 + 4 = 6. If you subtract 22 instead, you get 2, and the row 12 / 12 / 6 turns into 12 / 12 / 2. The same goes for the year: 1999 → 28 → 10 here, and 6 by subtraction. If the numbers do not match, check the reduction rule first and the interpretations second.

faq.q: Is Manipura different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, so a man and a woman with the same date of birth have the same numbers.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice and 11 Strength?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. In Waite’s deck and in many Tarot books these two cards are swapped. So an interpretation is checked by the card’s name, not by its number: the meaning rests on the name.

items.title: Svadhisthana
level: Svadhisthana answers for joy, children and creative work — for everything done not by calculation but because you want to. The level is often underrated, yet it is what holds motivation up: without it any correct life turns into hard labour within a year.

The check is simple: when did the person last do something with no aim and no use in it? A strong column gives a taste for life and ease in the body; a blocked one gives “I have no time”, shame about pleasure, and rest that looks like lying down with a phone and gives nothing back.

Where this level stands in the chart: the left number is the entry of the money line, point L, and the right one the entry of relationships and the karmic tail, point M. Both lie on the inner rhombus, level with the centre. Hence the sense of the row: joy is not a separate topic here, it is what pays for both work and closeness.

The right number has a quirk you can spot at once on your own chart: point M only ever carries numbers divisible by three — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 and 21. Nothing else lands there, whatever the date of birth. The left number is free and takes any value from 3 to 22, so the pair almost never matches, and it has to be read as two different questions rather than one.

article.title: Svadhisthana in the destiny matrix: where the chakra of desire sits and what its three arcana say
article.short: Svadhisthana is the second chakra from the bottom, the chakra of desire and pleasure. In the destiny matrix it answers three questions: what truly draws you, what you turn your desire into, and what feeling stays with you afterwards. On the chart it sits below and to the right, hard up against the centre. Physics is the inner right point L, energy the inner bottom point M, and emotions their sum, point R, where the money and relationship lines cross. It is the only chakra whose three numbers all lie on those two lines: in the matrix, desire is the common source of how a person earns and how they love. And one more property that almost nobody writes about: the energy of Svadhisthana is always a multiple of three. Everyone has one of seven cards there — The Empress, The Lovers, The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Devil, The Moon or The World.

intro: You will see your three Svadhisthana numbers straight after the calculation by date of birth — free and with no sign-up. The other six chakras are there too.

sections.h2: Where Svadhisthana is in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The destiny matrix is an octagram made of two squares. Point A (day of birth) is on the left, B (month) at the top, C (year) on the right and D (the sum of the first three) at the bottom. In the middle is the centre, E. Between each outer point and the centre lie the inner points. Svadhisthana takes the two closest to the centre: one on the right-hand ray and one on the bottom ray. Its third number is point R between them, in the lower right sector.

So the question “where is Svadhisthana in the destiny matrix” has two answers. On the chart: below and to the right of the centre, at points L and M and in the triangle between them. In our chakra table: the second row from the bottom, between Muladhara and Manipura. From support we move to desire, and from desire to action.

The chakra table is a staircase across the points of the chart. It descends from the outer points on the left and at the top (Sahasrara) to the centre (Manipura), then comes back out to the outer points on the right and at the bottom (Muladhara). There are four steps above the centre and only two below it. Svadhisthana is the only step between the centre and the lower corners of the chart, where material task C and karmic task D stand.

paragraphs.h3: How to work out Svadhisthana by hand

paragraphs: There is only one rule: any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits until it is 22 or less. Example: 31 March 1993.

ol: **A**, the day arcanum: 31 → 3 + 1 = 4.
**B**, the month: 3.
**C**, the year arcanum: 1 + 9 + 9 + 3 = 22.
**Emotions** = physics + energy = 8 + 15 = 23 → 5.

paragraphs: The Svadhisthana row is **8 / 15 / 5**: Justice, The Devil, The Hierophant. Gender plays no part in the calculation.

If another calculator gave you different numbers, check three things. Is the column order the same: physics, energy, emotions? Is the year reduced by adding its digits (1993 → 22) rather than by taking a remainder? And does the site use the same chart? Here the calculation follows Natalia Ladini’s classic matrix with points A–T, while some sites use other chakra formulas.

sections.h2: What Svadhisthana is and what it stands for
paragraphs: The name is built from the Sanskrit sva, “one’s own, self”, and adhishthana, “base, dwelling place”. It is usually translated as “one’s own abode” or “the place where your ‘I’ is established”. Western books call it the sacral chakra. The Sanskrit name fits the theme exactly. Desire is the most personal thing a person has: nobody can want something on command, whether the command is someone else’s or their own.

The chakra is described in detail in the treatise Shat-chakra-nirupana (16th century). In 1919 Arthur Avalon translated it into English in his book The Serpent Power. There Svadhisthana is a six-petalled lotus “of a beautiful vermilion colour”, and inside it lie a white region of water shaped like a half-moon and the syllable vam. The familiar orange came much later, from the Western “rainbow” scheme of the chakras, which is usually traced back to a 1977 book by Christopher Hills.

In tarot, chakras are used by Benebell Wen, for one, in her book Holistic Tarot (2015). In her seven-chakra spread the second card indicates the “emotional plane, creativity, any artistic endeavors”, hopes and fears, and also sex and sexuality. The destiny matrix works differently: instead of one drawn card there are three calculated arcana. But the circle of themes is much the same.

In the reading on our site, the theme of Svadhisthana is **desire and pleasure**. Not duty or discipline, but “I want”: what pulls you, what you do purely out of interest, how you allow yourself joy, closeness, creativity and rest — and what feeling you come away with. The chakra’s element is water, and the metaphor works. Desire flows. Dam it with prohibitions, and one day it bursts through. Let it run without banks, and it spreads out and grows shallow. Water does best where it has a riverbed.

Popular readings also call Svadhisthana “the chakra of children”. The link runs through creativity and play: through whatever is born of desire, be it a drawing, a garden, a business or a family. But how many children a person will have, or whether they will have any at all, is something no formula of the matrix calculates.

sections.h2: Three numbers, three questions about desire
paragraphs: **Energy (M) — what draws you.** This is the engine. It switches desire on before any decision is made: beauty, excitement, quiet, mystery, another person. You do not choose your energy — you notice it.

**Physics (L) — what you do with desire.** What the pull turns into in practice: a pastime, rest, creative work, closeness, spending. This is where you can see whether you let desire into your life, and in what form.

**Emotions (R) — what stays afterwards.** Satisfaction, warmth, pride — or guilt, emptiness, “what a waste”. This number comes from the first two, and there is logic in that: the aftertaste depends both on what you wanted and on how you went about getting it.
On the site the columns run in the order “physics / energy / emotions”, but it is easier to read them starting from energy. First you want, then you act, then you feel.

**The one-evening test.** Recall a free evening that went well. What drew you to that particular pastime? That is energy. What did you actually do? That is physics. What feeling did you wake up with the next morning? That is emotions. Read against a single episode, the three arcana come alive. Read one by one, they shrink into three little horoscopes.
When people say their Svadhisthana “isn’t working”, they usually mean one of three breakdowns, and each falls in its own column.

ul: **“I don’t know what I want.”** A break in energy: the pull is there, but muffled — by duty, tiredness, the habit of wanting what you are supposed to want. The person rests “like everyone else” and cannot understand why the rest does nothing for them.
**“I want it, but later.”** A break in physics: the desire is known but not let into life. Or let in only on a schedule. Or in a loop: forbid it for a long time, then snap.

**“I did it, and there was no joy.”** A break in emotions: the pleasure was had, but afterwards come guilt, emptiness or anxiety. It looks as if it was bought at a price you never agreed on with yourself.

paragraphs: What such a break looks like in your case is shown by your three arcana: in the full reading, the difficulty of each row is derived from its combination rather than taken from a general list.

**energy M** is the first number of the relationship line M–R1–R and of the karmic tail M–N–D;
**emotions R** is the last number of both lines, the point where they cross.

paragraphs: From here on, this is our reading, not a rule of the method.

If desire and money start at the same point, then one card describes both your favourite pastime and the action your earning starts with. For the row 8 / 15 / 5 that card is Justice: both pleasure and the first money impulse go through fair measure, with how much, when and for what agreed in advance.

If desire and closeness start at the same point, then one and the same card describes what attracts you in pastimes and what attracts you in people. The Devil in energy is a pull towards the strong and the gripping, towards whatever “won’t let go”. By this logic it works both in hobbies and in the choice of the people you get close to.

And the emotions of Svadhisthana stand where money and love cross. The feeling left after pleasure rarely stays in one area. Guilt over a purchase spoils an evening with someone close. And the joy of rest shared with someone makes you more generous with spending too.

So when something keeps repeating in money or in relationships, it helps to ask not only “how do I earn?” and “whom do I choose?”, but also “what do I allow myself, and how do I feel about it afterwards?”

paragraphs.h3: If you know your karmic tail

paragraphs: Then you already know the energy of your Svadhisthana: it is the first number of the tail.

head: Svadhisthana energy
Karmic tails that start with it

paragraphs: One number, different roles. In the tail, M is the entry into an old script that replays by itself. In Svadhisthana the same card is the engine of desire. On the chart the tail runs along the bottom ray from point M to point D, that is, from the energy of Svadhisthana to the energy of Muladhara. Our image: the old script is stretched between desire and support, and it is set off by the very pull that gives you strength in Svadhisthana.

paragraphs.h3: Svadhisthana grows out of the centre

paragraphs: Both its points are counted from the centre E: L = C + E, M = D + E. In the matrix the centre is the comfort zone, the state you return to when nothing is asked of you. In our reading, Svadhisthana shows what that state wants from the world: in the material sphere, through point C, and in the karmic one, through point D. Hence a practical conclusion: if the “right” kind of rest does not restore you, perhaps it simply does not suit your centre.

sections.h2: Why Svadhisthana’s energy is always a multiple of three
paragraphs: Whoever you are, the energy of your Svadhisthana is one of seven numbers: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21. The other fifteen arcana never appear in this column.

The reason lies in the arithmetic of reduction. Adding up digits keeps the remainder after division by 9 (the old school trick of “casting out nines” rests on this). Take the sum of the first three arcana, S = A + B + C. Point D carries the remainder of S, the centre E = S + D the remainder of 2S, and the energy M = D + E that of 3S. And a number with the same remainder as 3S is always divisible by three.
The same arithmetic gives two more facts:

ul: **The Magician (1) and The High Priestess (2) never appear in Svadhisthana**, in any of its three columns. Each of its numbers is the reduced sum of two arcana, and here such a sum is always greater than two. And reducing the numbers from 23 to 44 gives 3 to 12.

**There are only 135 possible rows.** Physics takes 20 values and energy 7, but five pairs never occur for anyone: 3 and 3, 3 and 9, 4 and 3, 4 and 9, 4 and 12. This was checked by going through every date from 1900 to 2100.

paragraphs.h3: Find your Svadhisthana energy in a minute

paragraphs: The energy depends only on the sum of the first three arcana, so you can find it without a calculator.

ol: **The day arcanum** is your day of birth. If it is above 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 31 → 4.
**The month** is its number, from 1 to 12.
**The year arcanum** is the sum of the year’s digits. If that comes out above 22, add again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 1993 → 22.
Add the three numbers and **do not reduce** the sum. Find it in the table.

paragraphs: **Each decade has its own pattern.** In calculations for dates from the 1940s, the Devil or the Moon stands in Svadhisthana’s energy in almost half of all cases (49.7%). For dates from the 1990s it is 42%, and for the 2000s only a third (32.8%). There the Hermit has moved into first place: 18.7%, against 9.1% for the forties. And the Empress turns up four times as often for them as for their grandparents. The reason, again, is arithmetic: the years of the 21st century have small digit sums (2004 → 6), so the sums S shift. This is a property of the calendar, not a verdict on a generation.
Energy is one number out of three. Physics also depends on the year arcanum, and emotions on both numbers at once. The calculator will show the full row and the other six chakras in a second.

sections.h2: The seven energies of Svadhisthana: what draws you
paragraphs: In other chakras any arcanum can turn up as energy; here only seven can. That is why more can be said about each of them than in a general reference: what sets a person with this card in energy going, how it looks in life, and where the same pull starts to get in the way. Under each card are the titles of two rows with this energy from our full reading.

paragraphs.h3: 3 · The Empress — wanting things to grow

paragraphs: One date in 17, and among dates after 2000, one in 9.

Waite writes that in certain aspects the Empress has been “correctly described as desire and the wings thereof”, but that she is “above all things universal fecundity”: a field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond it there is a fall of water. Wen sees her as the card of creativity and fruition, of an idea carried through to harvest. In the energy of Svadhisthana, this is desire that wakes up next to whatever is alive and growing. You are set going by what can be grown, cooked, arranged or decorated: a garden, a kitchen, a home, a business gaining strength before your eyes. Your pleasure is generous and tangible — taste, smell, colour, a laden table.

The trap is growing things for everyone but yourself. The Empress easily turns pleasure into care: you feed, arrange and delight, and put off your own “I want” until everyone else is happy. The second trap is abundance that is never enough: one more vegetable bed, one more dish, one more project. Desire needs a harvest, not endless sowing.
In the reading: “Slowing down in your own little paradise” (12-3-15), “Sowing generously without knowing what will grow” (19-3-22).
Found in roughly one calculation in nine.

For Waite this is “in all simplicity the card of human love”: a man and a woman stand “unveiled before each other”. Wen adds the theme of a choice in which heart and mind may not agree, and the tree behind the woman, she says, symbolises “the desire for sensation”. In the energy of Svadhisthana, desire comes alive next to another person. Pleasure doubles when it is shared: a holiday together, a joint project, an evening when your tastes matched. People and beauty draw you, and what interests you most is what can be shared.

The trap is checking your desire against someone else’s. “Will they like it?” — and soon you like whatever your partner likes, while your own taste falls silent. The flip side of the same card is two desires you cannot choose between. Then pleasure is put off until the choice makes itself.
In the reading: “Shared joy, split down the middle” (8-6-14), “Let someone close into your twilight” (18-6-6).

paragraphs.h3: 9 · The Hermit — wanting something of your own

paragraphs: One date in eight, and for the 2000s the most common energy: almost one date in five.

Waite calls the Hermit “a card of attainment”. His lantern with its star is held up “on an eminence”, and the beacon’s message is “where I am, you also may be”. Waite says plainly that the card is understood “quite incorrectly” when it is tied to “the idea of occult isolation”. Wen describes someone who “sees the world through his or her own light” and “walks in the direction of his own thoughts only”. In the energy of Svadhisthana, desire switches on in quiet and in depth. You are set going by a path of your own: a long pursuit done alone, mastery, a subject you can dive into headfirst. Your pleasure needs no audience; it needs depth.

The weak spot is that a joy nobody sees is easy to put off forever. Or to hide: “I’ll show it once it’s finished.” Solitude turns from a place where you fill up into a shelter from other people’s wishes and judgements. Yet the Hermit holds up his lantern so that others can see the light too.
In the reading: “Refine it in silence, then give it away” (8-9-17), “Walk into the dark with your own lantern” (18-9-9).

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man — wanting to stop and see things differently

paragraphs: Found in roughly one calculation in seven.

Waite stresses that the tree the man hangs from is “living wood”, and that his face expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”. This is “life in suspension, but life and not death”. Wen sees in the Hanged Man “seeing the same issues as others, but through a different perspective”, and assigns the card to the element of Water. Of the seven possible energies of Svadhisthana, only two are Water cards for Wen: the Hanged Man and the Moon. In the energy of Svadhisthana, desire lives in the pause. You are set going by the chance to go still, lose track of time and see the familiar from an unusual side. Pleasure comes when nobody is hurrying you: watching water, rereading, taking things apart, turning the usual upside down.

This is not a card of patience. Its trouble lies elsewhere: a pause that ought to be entrancement becomes waiting for permission. “I’ll rest once everything is done.” Pleasure is put off, then sacrificed to tasks altogether — and if it does happen after all, it feels like guilt.
In the reading: “Stopping to love the familiar anew” (12-12-6), “Let the water guide the brush” (18-12-3).
Almost one date in four — the most common energy in calculations for the 20th century.

On Waite’s card a man and a woman stand chained at an altar. Their tails are animal, but “there is human intelligence in the faces”, and he who is exalted above them “is not to be their master for ever”. Wen describes the Devil as attachment and the temptation of the senses, a “preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification”. In the energy of Svadhisthana, this is strong, bodily, insistent desire: taste, speed, excitement, things, sensations, “more”. The engine is powerful. You know how to want, and that gives you passion, energy and the ability to throw yourself into something completely.

The trap is that desire starts setting conditions. You want more even when there is almost no pleasure left. Or a seesaw sets in: hold out for a long time, snap, blame yourself, hold out again. The card’s main question is who is master of whom: you of your desire, or your desire of you. On its own, the card speaks of neither vice nor addiction. It is simply the most common energy of Svadhisthana, found in almost a quarter of calculations.
In the reading: “A tamed pull and honest scales” (11-15-8), “A wild side free of shame” (18-15-6).

paragraphs.h3: 18 · The Moon — wanting what beckons from afar

paragraphs: Found in roughly one calculation in five.

Waite calls the Moon “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”. The path on the card is lit only by “reflected light”, and Waite ends with “Peace, be still”, the words that calm a storm. Wen writes of “poetry and mystery”, of a tame side and a wild side that “are at odds”, and of the Moon as a force that pulls on water, like the tide. In the energy of Svadhisthana, desire is born of an image, a mood, an atmosphere: music, night, water, stories, riddles, roles. Often you want not the thing itself but the image of it. In return, you sense atmosphere as few others do and can turn an ordinary evening into a small piece of magic.

The catch is wanting the picture rather than the thing. You get it — and it is not what you imagined. Or fantasy becomes a way of not facing an uncomfortable question: pleasant while it lasts, murky afterwards. The test for lunar energy is simple: what is left in the morning.
In the reading: “A firm map for a misty land” (4-18-22), “Living by the tides of interest” (10-18-10).
Found in roughly one calculation in eight.

For Waite the World is “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”, “the rapture of the universe”, the day “when the morning stars sang together”. In his list of divinatory meanings, “voyage, route” and “change of place” stand side by side. Wen calls the World a card of completion and “the card of synthesis”. In the energy of Svadhisthana, this is a pull towards fullness and variety: the road, new tastes, the whole picture, the closed circle. You are set going by bringing different things together — cuisines from different countries, old friends and new ones, pursuits that others think cannot go together. Pleasure comes at the moment of completion: the last piece of the puzzle, the route travelled, the whole that has fallen into place.

The trap is wanting everything at once. Attention spreads thin, choosing one thing is hard, and completion is put off for the sake of a perfect wholeness that never comes. The World brings joy when the circle does close, even if it is smaller than you wanted.
In the reading: “Bringing together everything you love” (21-21-6), “Experience the world in every element” (22-21-7).

paragraphs: The table gives the words, but not the meaning of the row. Justice in physics next to the Devil in energy means one thing; next to the Hermit, something else entirely. How exactly is shown in the examples below.

**Mirror rows: X-18-X.** In the arithmetic of the matrix, the Moon behaves like water: add 18 to any number from 5 to 11, reduce it, and you get the same number back (7 + 18 = 25 → 7). So there are seven rows in which emotions repeat physics: from 5-18-5 to 11-18-11. There are a lot of them: roughly one date in eight in 1940–2012, and in the forties almost one in five. Four of the six most common Svadhisthana rows are mirror rows. Our reading: what you do is what you feel afterwards, only now as a reflection in water. The Chariot in physics is movement towards a goal; the Chariot in emotions is the triumph of a path found.

**Physics matches energy.** This happens in six rows: 6-6-12, 9-9-18, 12-12-6, 15-15-3, 18-18-9, 21-21-6 — roughly one calculation in 24. Here one card holds two positions, and that is not a doubling of the quality. In energy it describes what draws you; in physics, how you handle it. In our reading, desire here goes into action almost without translation, which makes the feeling that stays afterwards matter all the more.

**The most common and the rarest.** In calculations for dates from 1940–2012, the most common row is 11-15-8, about once in 44 dates. It is followed by 10-15-7, 10-18-10, 7-18-7 and 9-18-9. The rarest are 9-3-12, 21-3-6 and 22-21-7: about one date in a thousand.

sections.h2: How to read your own row: 8 / 15 / 5 worked through
paragraphs: Take the same date, 31.03.1993. The Svadhisthana row is Justice, The Devil, The Hierophant.

ol: **Energy — The Devil.** The pull is strong and clinging: it promises pleasure right away and lets go reluctantly.

**Physics — Justice.** On Waite’s card she sits between pillars with a sword and scales. Hence the way of handling desire: neither forbidding it nor giving in to it, but weighing it and giving it a place — after the work is done, at the proper time.
**Emotions — The Hierophant.** The evening you spent is afterwards checked against the rules you have taken in, and you are at peace if the fun fitted within them.
**One connecting thought.** A strong pull, a fair measure and rules taken to heart come together in one point: desire needs not a bridle but a place set aside for it in advance.

paragraphs: This is how the row reads in the full reading:
**Striking a deal with your own desire**

**A strong desire turns into joy when it has a place set aside for it in advance.** A new series is bound to pull you in — so it gets Saturday. All week things run their usual course, and Saturday becomes a small celebration with its own ritual: a pot of tea, a blanket, the phone left in another room. The pleasure is whole: it hasn’t been stolen from your duties, it breaks no promise, and so it leaves no bitter aftertaste.

It gets harder when every pleasure has to be earned first — then it fades before it has even begun. And the pull doesn’t always keep to the terms: you stay up until three, spend more than you meant to — and straight away comes a stern “that’s not how it’s done”. The rules get tighter, desire builds up pressure, and after a while it all happens again. Pleasure turns into a ledger of debts: what was allowed, what was broken, how to pay it back. In all this bookkeeping there’s hardly any room left for the joy itself.
The Devil stands in energy in almost a quarter of calculations, yet the rows that contain it read quite differently. The neighbours decide everything.

In the second, Strength tames the excitement, and Justice arrives only afterwards, in the feeling: did the scales balance, was anyone short-changed? In the third comes the Hanged Man’s pause: savouring slowly until the strong pull turns into the Hermit’s quiet knowledge of what you really want. One and the same card, three different ways of wanting. That is why reading a single arcanum will never replace reading the row.

sections.h2: Your Svadhisthana and the other six chakras
paragraphs: Seven chakras, three arcana in each: physics, energy, emotions. The numbers are visible straight after the free calculation, and the interpretations open in the full reading — until you pay, the rows are locked.

Svadhisthana is one row out of seven. Above it is Manipura: will and independence, from the same centre E. Below it is Muladhara: support, from the outer points C and D — the very points on whose rays Svadhisthana stands. Desire rarely lives on its own. It leans on what you count as your support and is tested by how much will you have.
For your date, the chakra part of the full reading contains:

ul: **seven sections, from Muladhara to Sahasrara**, each with its own title, main idea and captions for the three arcana: what role each one plays in that chakra;

**three connected paragraphs per chakra**: the theme of the chakra and what each card brings to it, a picture of how the combination looks in life, and the difficulty that grows out of the same combination;
**a separate text for each of the 135 possible Svadhisthana rows** — not three dictionary meanings glued together, but an interpretation of that exact row.

paragraphs: The chakra reading is part of the full matrix reading, together with the other sections and the printable report.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, Svadhisthana physics L = C + E, energy M = D + E, emotions R = L + M. Every sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All the numerical facts — energy being a multiple of three, the 135 possible rows, the absence of 1 and 2, the frequencies of rows and energies, the shift between generations — were obtained by going through every date from 1900 to 2100. Shares are given for all birth dates from 1940–2012.
**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the authors’ original English.
**Tradition** — the Shat-chakra-nirupana in Arthur Avalon’s translation (The Serpent Power, 1919). The “rainbow” colours of the chakras are a Western scheme from the second half of the 20th century.

Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix. The “physics / energy / emotions” columns, the reading of the seven energies, and the link between Svadhisthana and money, relationships and the tail are the author’s interpretation.

This is a symbolic model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a medical description. The numbers say nothing about the body, sex life or future events, and they do not determine whether chakras are “open”.

faq.q: Where is Svadhisthana in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Below and to the right of the centre. Physics is the inner point on the right ray (L, between the year C and the centre), energy the inner point on the bottom ray (M, between the karmic task D and the centre). Emotions are point R between them, where the money and relationship lines cross. In our chakra table it is the second row from the bottom, right above Muladhara.

faq.q: My energy is The Devil (15) or The Moon (18) — is that bad?
faq.a: No. These are the two most common energies of Svadhisthana: together they occur in 43% of calculations for dates from 1940–2012. The Devil in energy speaks of strong desire, not of vice. The Moon speaks of desire born of an image and a mood, not of living in illusions. Each card has its own trap, but a calculated number is never “reversed” and hands out no marks. What becomes of the energy depends on how it combines with physics and emotions.

faq.q: Does Svadhisthana say anything about sexuality and children?
faq.a: About sexuality — as part of the theme of desire and pleasure: in Wen it is explicitly part of the second position of the chakra spread. But the numbers do not describe a person’s intimate life and give it no marks. About children — no. Svadhisthana is called “the chakra of children” because of creativity and play, but the matrix does not calculate how many children there will be, whether they will be boys or girls, or when.

faq.q: How can you tell if Svadhisthana is “blocked” or “in the minus”?
faq.a: From the numbers, you can’t. In this calculation everyone has all three columns filled, and an arcanum number is the name of a symbol, not a score. What popular readings call “the minus” is usually one of three breakdowns: I don’t know what I want; I want it but don’t allow myself; I allowed myself and felt guilty afterwards. It is more useful to find where the chain breaks for you than to hunt for a “blocked” chakra.

faq.q: Are Svadhisthana’s energy and the karmic tail the same thing?
faq.a: The number is the same: the energy of Svadhisthana always equals the first number of the tail, because both are taken from point M. But the triples are different and are read differently. The tail M–N–D describes a script that replays by itself. The Svadhisthana row describes how you want, what you do with desire and what you feel afterwards. The match only means that the old script and your desire are set going by one and the same card.

faq.q: Is Svadhisthana connected with money?
faq.a: In this scheme, directly. The physics of Svadhisthana is the first number of the money line, and its emotions are the last. Our reading: the way you allow yourself pleasure and the way your money starts are described by one card. That is why a ban on joy often echoes in income, and pleasure with guilt attached in spending. These numbers cannot predict how much you will earn.

faq.q: Is Svadhisthana different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, and the numbers do not change with it. Popular readings like to split Svadhisthana into “feminine sensuality” and “masculine drive”, but these are stereotypes, not arithmetic. Any of the seven energies can turn up in anyone.

faq.q: Can you change your Svadhisthana?
faq.a: The numbers do not change: they are derived from the date of birth. What changes is how you use them. The Devil can keep you on a leash, or it can give you a passion for your work. The Moon can lead you off into fantasies, or it can make an ordinary day magical. The Hanged Man can keep putting joy off, or it can teach you to savour it. The row shows both the trap and the strength of one and the same desire.

items.title: Muladhara
level: Muladhara is the support: the body, a home, money for the month ahead, the feeling of standing on solid ground. It is the lowest level of all, and it holds up every other one — without it the higher meanings hang in the air and any plan gets derailed by everyday chores.

A strong Muladhara looks unremarkable from the outside: the person sleeps, eats, pays the bills and does not panic at the word “crisis”. A weak one brings constant worry about tomorrow even when money is fine, the habit of living out of a suitcase, and a body that gets attention last of all.
items.personal_intro: Everyday support: how you organise daily life, what motivates you to maintain it and how secure you feel.

columns.title: Physics
columns.text: The most literal column of the three: body, stamina, a place to live, money left in the account. It shows whether a person has a foundation solid enough to build something lasting on.

columns.title: Energy
columns.text: Gives staying power and the ability to hold on when everything is falling apart. A full column means a person gets back on their feet with sleep and a proper meal; an empty one means a single conversation drains them and every change of season knocks them out of action.

columns.title: Emotions
columns.text: This is about the basic sense of safety. At its best it gives calm and trust in life; at its worst, a fear of not having enough, which makes a person accept bad terms and then cling to them.

article.title: The Muladhara chakra in the destiny matrix: what keeps you grounded
article.short: Muladhara is the first chakra, the root. In the destiny matrix it stands for your footing: home, daily life, money to live on, the familiar rhythm of your days. It is everything you stand on, and what you do when the ground shifts under your feet. Three arcana describe Muladhara. Physics sits at the right-hand point of the matrix: it is the arcanum of your birth year. Energy sits at the bottom point: the sum of the day, the month and the year. Emotions are the sum of the first two numbers. Any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Together the three arcana answer one question: what gives you a sense of home, and what shakes it. You can work out your Muladhara in a minute without a calculator. Below you will find the formula, a table by year of birth and the meaning of each arcanum in each column.

intro: The arcana of Muladhara and the other six chakras appear as soon as you calculate. Free, with no sign-up.

sections.h2: What Muladhara is and why everything starts with it
paragraphs: The name comes from Sanskrit and translates almost word for word: mula means root, adhara means support. In Indian tradition it is the first and lowest of the seven chakras, linked with the element of earth. Benebell Wen, author of one of the best-known modern tarot textbooks, calls the Muladhara position in her chakra spread **“the foundation card”**: “what roots the Seeker”. Among other things, she reads it for a sense of security, stability and belonging.

Muladhara is the base of the chart. It comes first in our table and in the reading: first what gives you a sense of home, then desire, action, relationships, words, understanding and meaning. The logic is simple: while there is no ground under your feet, it is hard to think about anything else.
Muladhara answers some very down-to-earth questions:

ul: where, and with whom, you truly feel at ease;
how your household runs and who is responsible for what;
how you handle money for everyday living, your belongings and your reserves;
what you do first when your footing gives way: a move, a lost job, a divorce, a renovation, a debt, the birth of a child;
what you hold on to more tightly than you should.

paragraphs: What Muladhara in the matrix does not show: how much you earn, whether you own a flat, or the state of your body. The numbers describe how you stand on the ground, not how much ground you own.

sections.h2: Where Muladhara sits in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The matrix is an eight-pointed star made of two squares. The first, the personal square, stands on its corner like a diamond. On its left is the arcanum of your day of birth (A), at the top the month (B), on the right the year (C), and at the bottom the sum of these three numbers (D). The second, the family square, places its corners between them. Point E sits in the centre.

Muladhara occupies the **right-hand and bottom corners** of the personal square: C is physics, D is energy. Emotions are the sum of C and D, and on the chart this is the same number that stands in the corner of the family square between them, at point H. So the whole of Muladhara lies along one stretch of the outer ring, in the lower right sector of the star.

The diagram shows how the whole chakra table is built. The top chakra, Sahasrara, sits on the opposite edge of the star: its numbers are the day, the month and corner F between them. The other five chakras run diagonally through the centre. Manipura is the centre itself, while Svadhisthana, Muladhara’s neighbour, sits on the inner points of the same sector, closer to the centre. Even the point labels mirror each other: corner F at Sahasrara is the Spiritual male family line, and corner H at Muladhara is the Material male family line.
Three more coincidences that rarely get written about:

ul: **Muladhara’s energy is the root of the karmic tail.** The tail runs down the lower ray to point D, so its last number always equals Muladhara’s energy.
**Svadhisthana grows out of Muladhara.** Its physics is Muladhara’s physics plus the centre of the chart, and its energy is Muladhara’s energy plus the centre.

**On the age scale, all three Muladhara numbers stand in a row**: C covers ages 40–50, H 50–60, D 60–70. This is a property of the diagram, not a forecast. Still, the coincidence is curious: on the same scale Sahasrara takes up the first three decades of life.

sections.h2: How to calculate your Muladhara by date of birth
paragraphs: All you need is the date and the reduction rule: if a number is greater than 22, add its digits, and repeat until you get a number from 1 to 22. In this system 22 is the Fool (not 0), 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength.

ol: **Physics.** Add up the digits of your birth year: 1985 → 1 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 23 → 2 + 3 = 5.
**Energy.** Add the day, the month and physics. If the day is over 22, reduce it first: 23 → 5, 28 → 10, 31 → 4.
**Emotions.** Add physics and energy.

paragraphs: You don’t even need to calculate the first number: just find your birth year in the table.

paragraphs.h3: Muladhara physics by year of birth

paragraphs: Each row is a decade, each column the last digit of the year. Take 1987: row “1980s”, column “…7”, physics 7, the Chariot.
This table leads to a few unexpected conclusions.

ul: **The first card of your Muladhara is shared with everyone born in the same year.** Everyone born in 1993 has the Fool in physics; in 1990 it is the Sun, in 1987 the Chariot. At the turn of the millennium it changes abruptly: for those born in 1999 it is the Wheel of Fortune, and in 2000 the High Priestess.

**The other two cards are yours.** They depend on the day and month, so a single year produces between 11 and 20 different triples. Across everyone born from 1900 to 2026 there are 363 combinations. Even the most common of them, 19 / 6 / 7, falls on fewer than one date in a hundred.

**Some arcana almost never appear in Muladhara.** The Magician does not turn up here in any column for anyone born between 1900 and 2026. The High Priestess appears only in physics, and only for those born in 2000. Nobody born after 1930 has Death in physics, and nobody born after 1940 has Temperance. In energy and emotions both cards do occur.

**Energy is usually a small number.** In calculations for dates from 1950 to 2010, a number from 5 to 11 fills this column almost two times out of three. Each of the arcana from 13 to 16 accounts for only 1.5–2% of dates.
**In roughly one calculation in ten an arcanum repeats within Muladhara**, for example 7 / 7 / 14. A repeat does not double the quality: the same card works in two different roles.

paragraphs: Don’t feel like counting by hand? The calculator shows the whole table at once: seven chakras, three arcana in each.

sections.h2: Muladhara’s three numbers: what each one means
paragraphs: The columns are easiest to grasp through a single situation. Say your landlord asks you to move out within a month. Muladhara’s three numbers describe three layers of how you react.

ul: **Physics: what your hands start doing.** This is how your daily life and household are run. Someone with the Emperor in physics sits down with a spreadsheet of expenses. Someone with the Fool gives away half their things and browses listings in another neighbourhood with genuine curiosity. Someone with the Empress is already picturing where the plants will go in the new place.

**Energy: what drives you.** This is the motive behind building and protecting your footing, and the way you act when it gives way. One person needs to regain control, another to keep the partnership intact, a third to start with a clean slate, a fourth for everything to be fair.

**Emotions: the moment you start to feel calm.** This is your sense of safety. Some feel better once there is a plan. Some, when their own people are close. Some, when a way out appears or when everything has been fairly shared out.

paragraphs: Together the three columns give you a rough draft of a sentence about your footing: “I arrange my life like this (physics), because this matters to me (energy), and I feel calm when (emotions).” For 22 / 11 / 6 the draft reads: “I change my way of life easily and start over, because what matters to me is gently taming worry, and I feel calm when my loved ones are near.”

The draft is useful, but it is still just three meanings added together. The real reading begins when you see how the cards answer one another: where one supports another, where they pull in different directions and what comes of that in life. That is what the section after the card meanings is about.

sections.h2: Card by card: the meaning of each arcanum in Muladhara
paragraphs: Find each of your numbers in the right column. The heading gives the card’s overall theme in Muladhara, and below it is how the card sounds in each of the three roles. Every card has a side where it holds the ground and a side where it starts to get in the way. Both are given.
Arthur Edward Waite never wrote about chakras. But for some cards his 1910 book offers words that sound almost like a description of Muladhara. They are quoted here in his original English.

paragraphs.h3: 2 · The High Priestess — a footing built on what you quietly notice

paragraphs: Appears only in physics, and only for those born in 2000.

ul: **Physics.** Daily life rests on quiet observation. You remember where things let you down before, what runs out sooner than expected and what each person at home needs, and you take it all into account without a word. The shadow is keeping quiet about the household’s needs until the unsaid piles up.

paragraphs.h3: 3 · The Empress — a home where everything grows

paragraphs: Waite called her the Earthly Paradise, **“all that is symbolized by the visible house of man”**.

ul: **Physics.** A lived-in, warm, well-fed space: food, plants, supplies, guests. In a new place you quickly bring a home to life.

**Energy.** You want your footing to grow and multiply, so that everything around you flourishes and there is more than enough. When something wobbles, you start looking after people: feeding them, settling in, gathering everyone together.
**Emotions.** Calm when the house is full and the care flows both ways. Hurt when your work on making the home comfortable is taken for granted.

paragraphs.h3: 4 · The Emperor — master of your own ground

paragraphs: The first words Waite gives this card are **“Stability, power, protection, realization”**.

ul: **Physics.** A household run by rules: a budget, a routine, clarity about who is responsible for what. The home is in order and protected.
**Energy.** The need to have the final say over what is yours: money, housing, decisions. When the ground shifts, you are the first to take charge.
**Emotions.** The calm of an owner who has thought of everything. Anxiety when something slips out of control, even if there is no real threat.

paragraphs.h3: 5 · The Hierophant — a way of life proven by experience

ul: **Physics.** Daily life done the accepted way: family customs, holidays celebrated “properly”, rules about money you were taught as a child.

**Energy.** At a difficult moment you lean on what has stood the test of time: advice from your elders, the experience of someone who knows, a clear order of things. Among this card’s meanings Waite lists **“the man to whom the Querent has recourse”**: the person you turn to for help.
**Emotions.** Calm among your own people, when your way of life is accepted. Guilt appears when you want to live differently from the way things are done in your family.

paragraphs.h3: 6 · The Lovers — a footing chosen by two

ul: **Physics.** A home life built on mutual choice: a shared home, shared decisions, a life arranged together with someone close.
**Energy.** You want to build your footing with the person you have chosen. For the sake of the partnership you are ready to change your routine, move house, redraw your plans.
**Emotions.** Safety lies in reciprocity: being chosen and choosing for yourself. Anxiety comes when every decision about the home hinges on someone else’s approval.

paragraphs.h3: 7 · The Chariot — a home on the move

ul: **Physics.** Practical matters get sorted straight away: a breakdown, a move, repairs, with no delays and no lengthy preparation.
**Energy.** Providing for yourself under your own steam and holding your course. You rebuild your footing by acting, not by waiting.
**Emotions.** Confidence while the reins are in your hands and things are moving. Irritation when you have to wait, ask or stand still.
**Physics.** It is clear what belongs to whom and who pays for what. Arrangements about money and chores are spoken out loud.
**Energy.** The need for fair terms. When the balance is off, you recalculate, even out the contributions and agree on things afresh.
**Emotions.** Safe when everything is fair. Resentment over an unequal share is a sign that it is time to talk rather than let it build up.

paragraphs.h3: 9 · The Hermit — your own system, worked out alone

ul: **Physics.** Daily life arranged by your own judgement: nothing superfluous, your own logic, everything checked in person.
**Energy.** When your footing wobbles, you withdraw to think and look for your own answer rather than a ready-made tip.
**Emotions.** Calm in your own space and in the clarity of “I figured it out myself”. The shadow is loneliness, if you only feel safe far away from everyone.

paragraphs.h3: 10 · The Wheel of Fortune — stability in motion

ul: **Physics.** A flexible way of life that changes with circumstances: moves, different stages of life, uneven income.
**Energy.** Catching the turn and keeping your balance through change. You don’t cling to the old but adapt to the new rhythm.
**Emotions.** Relief when a way out appears. Unease when your footing depends on chance and on other people’s decisions.

paragraphs.h3: 11 · Strength — a firm but gentle hand

ul: **Physics.** Things run steadily and with care: no jolts and no overstrain, even when the load is heavy.
**Energy.** Holding your ground through patience rather than pressure. You don’t crush worry, you soothe it. On Waite’s card the lion has already been subdued and is led by a chain of flowers.
**Emotions.** The calm of self-possession: you know you will cope. The shadow is when “holding it together” becomes the only state you allow yourself.

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man — a footing in the pause

paragraphs: Rare in physics: only for those born in 1902, 1911, 1920 and 2019. Waite saw in this card **“life in suspension, but life and not death”**.

ul: **Physics.** A way of life that is “not like everyone else’s”, or a life lived through a time of transition. You know how to live when the familiar is on hold.
**Energy.** At a hard moment you don’t force your way through: you stop and look at the situation from another side. That is how you find a move that can’t be seen on the run.
**Emotions.** Calm in the pause: time in suspension doesn’t frighten you. The shadow is a pause with no next step.

paragraphs.h3: 13 · Death — the courage to close chapters

paragraphs: Nobody born after 1930 has it in physics. In energy and emotions it does occur. The card is about one stage giving way to the next, not about literal loss.

ul: **Physics.** Winding up a form of life that has run its course: moving out, clearing out, closing down.
**Energy.** A readiness to let go of what is spent in good time (things, housing, an old way of living) to make room for the new.
**Emotions.** Endings are felt deeply: sadness for what was and relief arrive together.

paragraphs.h3: 14 · Temperance — a household kept in measure

paragraphs: Nobody born after 1940 has it in physics. Yet Waite’s meanings for this card read like a straight description of a household Muladhara: **“Economy, moderation, frugality, management”**.

ul: **Physics.** A household rhythm you can keep up, in which old and new blend without sharp breaks.
**Energy.** Matching what you want with what is possible and steering clear of extremes. You put things right little by little rather than breaking them.
**Emotions.** The calm of having found the right measure. The shadow is dissatisfaction, if thrift rules out every wish.

paragraphs.h3: 15 · The Devil — a firm grip on the material

paragraphs: Waite’s list of meanings for this card opens with “ravage” and “violence” and ends with a caveat: **“that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”**.

ul: **Physics.** A strong pull towards comfort, possessions, everything you have built up. Matter holds on tight, and it is easy to grow attached to it.
**Energy.** The wish to own things securely. When a threat appears, your hands reach of their own accord for what feels solid: money, housing, familiar comfort.
**Emotions.** Pleasure in having enough and a strong attachment to what is yours. The shadow is fear of loss, when things become your only source of confidence.

paragraphs.h3: 16 · The Tower — the nerve to pull down what is unsound

ul: **Physics.** Clearing away what does not hold: shaky commitments, an impossible budget, a home where you are unhappy.
**Energy.** The resolve to change the foundation when the old one has stopped working. The key is to choose the change on the facts, not at the peak of irritation.
**Emotions.** A sharp response to upheaval, and a truth that only becomes visible after it.

paragraphs.h3: 17 · The Star — a home you first see in a dream

ul: **Physics.** Building towards what you long for: you see what the home could become and move towards it step by step.
**Energy.** Faith in the best, and generosity. You restore your footing through hope and by putting yourself into what is shared.
**Emotions.** Calm when there is a bright landmark ahead. Disappointment if today’s life keeps losing out to the perfect picture.

paragraphs.h3: 18 · The Moon — a footing when not everything is clear

ul: **Physics.** You notice what lies in the shadows of everyday life: unclear expenses, verbal agreements, hidden risks.
**Energy.** Sensitivity to the unknown. Your imagination is quick to paint dangers and helps you spot that something is wrong before others do.
**Emotions.** Anxiety about what cannot be seen. Light helps: pin down the terms, write down the figures, separate fact from guesswork.

paragraphs.h3: 19 · The Sun — a bright, open home

paragraphs: Waite’s meanings for this card: **“Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment”**.

ul: **Physics.** Simple, clear, hospitable daily life: a bright room, a laid table, joy in plain sight.
**Energy.** The wish to live in warmth and share it. You build your footing so that everyone around you is well.
**Emotions.** The calm of simple joy. The shadow is when other people’s approval becomes the measure of your home life.

paragraphs.h3: 20 · Judgement — hearing that it is time

paragraphs: Waite’s list of meanings for this card is very short: **“Change of position, renewal, outcome”**.

ul: **Physics.** Revisiting familiar rules, family ones included, and seeing clearly when a way of life is due for renewal.
**Energy.** Responding to an inner “it’s time”. You restore your footing with a decision that has long been coming.
**Emotions.** The relief of a new chapter and the warmth of a bond with your family. The shadow is the weight of duty to family overriding your own choice.

paragraphs.h3: 21 · The World — a life gathered into a whole

paragraphs: Among Waite’s meanings for this card are **“voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”**. For Muladhara this is an important hint: for the World, home can be a wide place.

ul: **Physics.** Fitting housing, work and travel into one life. Home can stretch across several cities and frequent trips.
**Energy.** The drive to bring everything together into a whole and close the circle of your affairs. Your footing is the sense that everything is in its place.
**Emotions.** The feeling of a settled life that has come together. The shadow is scattering yourself, when you want to keep every option open and choose none.

paragraphs.h3: 22 · The Fool — a footing that travels light

ul: **Physics.** Simple, mobile daily life, being quick to pack up, the courage to start from scratch.
**Energy.** The freedom to try something different. When something breaks, you don’t patch up the old, you start afresh.
**Emotions.** Relief in freedom and open roads. The shadow is unease, if freedom means constantly giving up stability.

sections.h2: One year, eleven different Muladharas
paragraphs: The Fool in the earth chakra is a paradox. Waite describes a young man who walks **“with light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him”**. And yet this card sits in Muladhara physics for everyone born in 1948, 1957, 1966, 1975, 1984 or 1993. How the Fool keeps his feet on the ground is decided by the other two cards.
Take 1993. Physics is the same for everyone, yet that year has eleven combinations. Here are a few headings from the full reading:

head: Muladhara
Arcana
Reading heading
rows: The Fool, The Empress, The Chariot
“A warm new home within a week”
The Fool, The Lovers, The Wheel of Fortune
“A footing that rests on the road”
“A foundation you can take with you”
The Fool, The Hanged Man, The Chariot
“Closing doors with no debts left behind”

paragraphs: The Fool is the same in every row: the ease with which a person changes their way of life. But the lives behind these rows could hardly be more different.

ul: With the Empress and the Chariot, the Fool turns a rented flat within a week into a home that smells of cooking, where the neighbour is already dropping in.
With the Lovers and the Wheel of Fortune, he shares one rucksack with someone close: money, plans and decisions are joint, so the couple takes the sharp turns with ease.
With the Emperor and Justice, a light-travelling household finds a master at the first emergency: the water is shut off, a plumber is on the way, and it is already clear who pays for what.
With Death and Justice, moving out becomes almost a ritual: the surplus given away, the landlord paid to the last penny, and a box of chocolates for the neighbour who watered the plants.

paragraphs: These combinations have their own difficulties, too. Where everything is shared, each person may end up with nothing of their own. Where the footing rests on the road, “I’ll settle in later” stretches into years, and the things go on living in boxes. And where doors close with no debts left behind, it is hard to put down roots: gratitude repaid at once never has time to grow into friendship. None of this follows from the dictionary meaning of the Fool. It appears only in the interplay of the three cards.

paragraphs.h3: This is what Muladhara looks like in the full reading

paragraphs: Date 31.03.1993. **Muladhara · Everyday support · 22 / 11 / 6**
**A foundation you can take with you**

head: Physics
Energy
Emotions
rows: 6 · The Lovers — calm beside your people

paragraphs: For you, home doesn’t start with walls or things. Your daily life follows the Fool: you travel light, ready to move, change the way you live and try something new. When the familiar order falls apart, Strength comes to the rescue: instead of rushing about, you calm your worry the way the woman on the card tames the lion — with a chain of flowers, not of iron. The Lovers bring the sense of safety: you feel at ease wherever your person is beside you and you’re open with each other.

The first evening in a new place: boxes still taped up, supper on the windowsill. Some people would be thrown by the chaos, but to you it already feels almost cosy — as long as someone close is there to laugh about the mess with you. **Your foundation isn’t a stockpile but calm and closeness, and you carry both with you.** A lease falls through, plans need rewriting — the worry comes but doesn’t take over, and your shared “us” soon brings back the feeling of home.

This foundation turns fragile when everything rests on one point. Living light can mean living without a cushion: savings “later”, paperwork “we’ll sort it out”. While things between you are steady, that’s not frightening. But then any falling-out hits harder than it should: you argue about the washing-up and feel anxious about everything at once. Out of habit you hide the fear behind calm, give way to keep the peace — and say nothing about what you need. Then your “us” holds up the whole home, which is too heavy a load for one bond.

Compare this with the draft from the section on the three columns. There, three meanings were strung together with commas. Here there is one idea you can recognise in your own life: **your foundation isn’t a stockpile but calm and closeness, and you carry both with you**. And the third paragraph shows where this strength becomes a weak spot: when the whole home rests on a single bond.

sections.h2: “Open”, “blocked”, “in the minus”: what Muladhara really shows
paragraphs: Plenty of articles about Muladhara list the signs of a “blocked” chakra and promise to “open” it. The destiny matrix can’t be read that way, and here is why.

ul: **The numbers are names of arcana, not scores.** 22 is not stronger than 3, and the Tower in Muladhara does not predict losing your home. There is no such thing as an empty Muladhara: everyone has three cards in it.

**“Plus” and “minus” are not different arcana but two modes of the same one.** The strength of your footing and its typical trap grow from one root. The trap begins where the strong side goes too far.
